pages.title: Guide
pages.description: The Mirage guide: what it is, how to run it, and the order to read the ten pages that cover detection, decoys, modes and operations.

sections.heading: What Mirage is
sections.text: Mirage is an open-source deception layer for public HTTP and HTTPS services: it detects automated reconnaissance — scanner noise, AI attack agents, opportunistic crawlers — and answers it with inert decoys that waste the scout's effort. It never breaks the site it protects: any internal failure sends traffic to the origin unmodified (I1), and decoys never reach search indexes, archives or ordinary visitors (I12). Enforcement — short, reversible, budget-capped bans — is opt-in and off by default (I9). Everything below is verifiable from the repository: the engine is pinned by the invariants and by golden vectors that every implementation must reproduce exactly.

sections.heading: What the guide covers
sections.text: Ten pages, written for an operator who has never run a honeypot and for an engineer who wants to audit one. Each page is self-contained; together they cover the whole system from first request to production runbook. Order Page What it answers 2 Getting started From a fresh clone to a running look-mode instance. 3 Architecture The decision path end-to-end, package by package. 4 Signals The 11 signals, their weights, and the gating rules. 5 Verdicts The verdict ladder with worked score arithmetic. 6 Decoys The catalog: personas, entries, leads, honeytokens. 7 Modes look, tripwires, protect — the operational ladder. 8 Tooling Every quality gate, lab and generator in the repo. 9 Operations The production runbook: stores, budgets, connectors. 10 Testing The test architecture and how to add a golden vector. 11 FAQ Twelve honest answers, including what Mirage cannot do.

sections.heading: Recommended reading order
sections.text: Operators deploying for the first time: getting started, then modes, then signals. That is enough to run look mode and read the dashboard with an accurate mental model of what the scores mean. Engineers auditing or extending: architecture, signals, verdicts, testing. These four pages map every claim to a package, a spec section and a test. Anyone considering enforcement: modes, operations and the FAQ, together with known limits — bans are single-address, short and budget-capped on purpose (I5, I15), and the honest answer to "does this stop attackers" is "it detects scouting and wastes attacker effort".

sections.heading: Beyond this guide
sections.text: Deploy guides — the from-zero path, the nginx transparent-proxy topology, and the Cloudflare Worker that runs at the edge. Reference — every config key, every CLI subcommand, the shared data files and the normative specs. Reading Mirage as an agent — the machine-readable surface (/llms.txt, /docs.json, --json outputs) for programs that consume this documentation. What Mirage will never do — hack-back, web poisoning, live credentials, indexable decoys — is recorded in the charter, not decided case by case.

pages.title: Getting Started
pages.description: From a fresh clone to a running look-mode Mirage instance: build, gates, minimal config, serve, and reading your first events.

sections.text: This page takes you from zero to a running look-mode instance. Look mode observes and records only — no decoys are served, nothing is enforced (I9) — so it is the safest starting point and the default. For the Cloudflare Worker deployment path, read the worker guide; this page covers the Go core and its CLI.

sections.heading: Prerequisites
sections.text: git and GNU make. Go 1.23 or newer — the module pins go 1.23.0. Python 3 with PyYAML — only for the golden-vector gate (tools/gen_vectors.py imports yaml). Node 20 or newer and npm — only for the worker package; no Go gate needs network access.

sections.heading: 1. Get the code and run every gate
sections.text: make check runs, in order: fmt-check (fails if any Go file is not gofmt-clean), vet (go vet ./...), build (go build ./...), test (go test -race ./...), vectors (regenerates the golden vectors and cross-checks the two independent sources in tools/gen_vectors.py; the generator exits 1 on any disagreement), and slop (the grep gate that rejects unfinished-work markers in code files). If make check is green you hold the same evidence CI produces on main — deterministic gates, not trust. See tooling for what each target runs.

sections.heading: 2. Write a minimal config
sections.text: mirage init writes a minimal valid config: mode: "look" and a generated dashboard_token — those two keys only; every other key keeps its documented default, and init loads the written file back through strict validation before reporting success. Init checks nothing else — the decoy-catalog path rules are enforced by the catalog loader at load time, not by init (see decoys). Open mirage.yaml and look at the two keys: dashboard_token — required, and required even though the default listen is loopback: an unauthenticated local endpoint is one curl away from a takeover. Init already generated one (crypto/rand); if you hand-write the file from mirage.example.yaml instead, generate one and paste it in: mode — leave it at look. Every key, default and bound is documented in the config reference. Loading is strict: a typo, an unknown key or a half-configured connector block is a boot-time error, never a silently disabled control. Validate before running: Exit 0 means every check passed; exit 1 means at least one failed, and the failure is named. Add --json for machine-readable output (see the CLI reference).

sections.heading: 3. Run it
sections.text: serve requires both the config and the upstream origin — there is no upstream key in the config, so the origin is always named explicitly. For a demo origin, serve the current directory on port 9000 in one terminal: Then run Mirage in front of it: Mirage runs two servers. The proxy binds listen (default 127.0.0.1:8080), scores every request that reaches it and forwards traffic to the upstream. The token-guarded dashboard binds its own loopback address, --dashboard-addr (default 127.0.0.1:8090; non- loopback binds are refused at startup). /healthz lives on the dashboard mux, so the liveness probe is: /healthz is the one tokenless endpoint — the load-balancer probe — with a fixed body and nothing else. The dashboard is loopback-only by design: on a remote host, tunnel it instead of opening it — ssh -L 8090:127.0.0.1:8090 you@example.com — and browse http://127.0.0.1:8090 from your workstation.

sections.heading: 4. Generate a benign request and a scanner path
sections.text: / answers 200 and /.env answers 404 — the proxy mirrors whatever the demo origin says, and neither request is scored: requests from loopback are never scored (I6) — they produce verdict observe, fire no signals and record no session state. The two curls prove the proxy and the fail-open path, nothing else. Scoring engages for requests from a real remote address. Point listen at an address a second machine can reach (for example listen: "192.168.1.10:8080"), restart serve, then from that machine: Score both requests the way the engine does. The first is ordinary: a bare curl sends three headers (Host, User-Agent, Accept), which fires headers_sparse (10, medium) — under the tag threshold of 15 — so the verdict is observe. The second matches data/scanner-paths.txt, firing scanner_path (25, high, SIG-101); that same-request signal ungates tooling_curl (15), and the sparse header set fires headers_sparse (10) too: request score 25 + 15 + 10 = 50. On the verdict ladder 50 is throttle territory, but in look mode the verdict is capped at tag and the action is always pass — the request reaches the origin unmodified (I1, I9). What changes is the record.

sections.heading: 5. Read the events
sections.text: The token also rides as Authorization: Bearer .... /api/events returns recorded decisions; each event carries ts_ms, session_key, method, path and the full decision — signals, request score, cumulative score, verdict, reason code. The other endpoints are /api/status, /api/sessions and /api/bans. Reason codes render in plain English from data/reason-texts.txt (I10). Where events go: emission is a bounded queue write that never blocks a request (I3); a drainer moves them into the store — SQLite in WAL mode at store.path (default mirage.db), kept for store.retention_days (default 30) — and the dashboard reads the store.

sections.heading: Where to go next
sections.text: Signals — what each score means. Modes — when to move up a rung. Deploy: nginx — the transparent-proxy topology for real traffic.

pages.title: Architecture
pages.description: The Mirage decision path end-to-end: adapter request to engine scoring, verdict ladder, actions, events, store and connectors.

sections.text: Mirage is one synchronous decision per request plus asynchronous everything else. That split is the architecture: the hot path is local and bounded (I3), every failure degrades to pass-through (I1), and every automated action leaves evidence (I10). This page walks the path once, then maps each step to its Go package.

sections.heading: The path of one request
sections.text: The figure below traces the full lifecycle at a glance: the synchronous decision from the client through the adapter, engine and verdict ladder to the action, then the asynchronous trail from the bounded event queue through the store to the connectors. {% include diagrams/decision-path.html %} Adapter submits a request. An edge adapter — Go middleware, the Cloudflare Worker, a future plugin — builds a model.Request: method, path (raw, including dot segments and query), client_ip, user_agent, header_count (all headers, including Host and User-Agent), has_cookie, ts_ms, and optionally auth_hint (credential material the adapter can see, matched against minted honeytokens). An adapter that cannot see a field passes the neutral value; signals requiring the field do not fire. client_ip is the adapter's own trusted-proxy walk result, never a raw spoofable header (I6). Service.Decide runs the fixed sequence (internal/service): The decision is timestamped once, so deadline arithmetic, ban bookkeeping and store records agree. Never-scored resolution (I6): owner, CDN and allowlisted-bot ranges, and verified-bot user agents, produce an observe decision with no session state recorded. Renewal (protect mode, enforcement armed): a request from an address holding an unexpired ban renews it — verdict ban, the ORIGINAL reason code, the remaining TTL, no signals, no rescore. A banned address must not earn its way out with clean-looking requests. Flipping the kill switch disarms renewal on the next decision (I9). The engine scores the request deterministically, in memory (I3), against the session snapshot: session key is sha256(client_ip):32, state expires after 30 idle minutes. Deadline check: if scoring overran the budget (5 ms), the decision is model.FailOpen() — verdict observe, action pass, reason SIG-000 — and no event is emitted. SIG-000 is reserved for fail-open and is never a ban input. Mode gating (I9): look caps the verdict at tag and always passes; tripwires keeps serve_decoy but passes throttle/ban actions; protect enforces, and a ban action goes through the gatekeeper. Deadline check again, after enforcement wiring; on overrun the adapter still sees the fail-open decision. Event emission: a bounded queue write that never blocks (I3). On a full queue the core drops the newest event and counts it — losing evidence is better than stalling a request. (The TypeScript worker's ring buffer drops the oldest instead; both engines keep the drop count.) The adapter acts on the returned model.Decision: pass (forward unmodified), serve_decoy (render the decoy named by decoy_id locally from the snapshot — never a network fetch), throttle (a local, capped slowdown), or ban (a short block, only when enforcement is enabled). Events drain to the store. A background drainer (internal/service) drains the queue every 250 ms in batches of 512, appends events, folds per-session rolling summaries (bounded at 65,536 sessions, least-recently- seen eviction) and upserts them. Stop flushes the queue once more. Bans fan out and reconcile. An applied ban is written to the gatekeeper, a renewal memo and the store, then handed to every connector on a bounded goroutine (5 s). A reconcile loop shows every connector the store's active ban set every 30 s, so a missed or crashed Apply heals and a revoked ban disappears from providers. Connectors are outbound-only and fail-open by design.

sections.heading: The packages
sections.text: Package Role on the path internal/model Shared types: Request, Decision, Event; session key; the trusted-proxy IP walk and never-scored ranges (I6); the reason-text sanitizer (I7). internal/config Strict YAML loading, every bound, the loopback token requirement; fails closed at boot. internal/detect The SIGNALS v1.1.0 engine: scoring, verdict ladder, gating; the parity target. internal/service Decide, renewal, mode gating, the drainer, the dashboard. Holds I1/I3/I9/I10 across packages. internal/decoy Catalog loader, deterministic renderer, pollution suite (I8, I12–I14). internal/enforce The gatekeeper: kill switch and per-verdict budgets (I5, I9). internal/events The bounded queue with drop policies and a drop counter (I3). internal/store SQLite (WAL) and in-memory stores; versioned schema. internal/connectors Denyfile, webhook, CrowdSec LAPI, Cloudflare — one retry envelope. packages/mirage-worker The TypeScript port: same engine and vectors, zero runtime dependencies, per-isolate state, fail-open handler.

sections.heading: Two implementations, one spec
sections.text: The Go core and the worker must produce identical verdicts on spec/golden-vectors/vectors.json (20 cases, 68 requests); CI fails on any divergence. The worker is stateless across isolates, so durable bans and long-horizon session signals belong to the core — a recorded limit in known limits. Continue with signals for what the engine actually measures.

pages.title: Signals
pages.description: The 11 detection signals of SIGNALS v1.1.0: what each one sees, its fixed weight and class, a concrete example, and its gating rules.

sections.text: A signal is one deterministic observation about a single HTTP request, made against an in-memory session snapshot — no network call, disk wait or LLM call is involved (I3). Weights, classes and reason codes are fixed by spec/SIGNALS.md v1.1.0; evaluation order is the table order 1→11, and a signal later in the order may read, but never change, the outcome of an earlier one. High-class signals can escalate; medium-class signals alone can never ban (I5).

sections.heading: The full table
sections.text: # id Weight Class Reason Fires when 1 scanner_path 25 high SIG-101 Normalized path matches data/scanner-paths.txt, or dot_escape fired 2 decoy_hit 30 high SIG-102 Path matches a decoy catalog entry 3 decoy_lead_follow 40 high SIG-103 Path matches a lead that exists only inside a decoy served earlier to this session 4 honeytoken_use 50 high SIG-104 Credential material in the request matches a honeytoken minted for a decoy served to this session 5 path_enumeration 25 high SIG-105 ≥ 8 distinct unknown paths in the trailing 60 s 6 ua_suspicious 15 medium SIG-106 User-Agent matches data/ua-suspicious.txt (case-insensitive substring) 7 ua_rotation 20 medium SIG-107 ≥ 4 distinct non-empty user agents in the trailing 300 s, AND gated (below) 8 no_cookie_persistence 15 medium SIG-108 ≥ 5 requests, never a cookie, cumulative score 0 before, no other signal this request 9 headers_sparse 10 medium SIG-109 header_count < 4 (all headers, including Host and User-Agent) 10 ua_missing 10 medium SIG-110 User-Agent absent or empty 11 tooling_curl 15 medium SIG-111 UA matches curl/, AND gated (below)

sections.heading: Reading the signals
sections.text: High class — path evidence. scanner_path (25) is the workhorse: GET /.env with any user agent fires it, as does a dot-segment escape such as /a/../../.. that clamps at the root. decoy_hit (30) fires when the path matches a catalog entry such as /admin/login; it is suppressed when scanner_path fired the same request — a scanner-list hit already fully explains the request. decoy_lead_follow (40) means the session asked for a path like /storage/logs/laravel-staging.log that only ever appeared inside a decoy it was served — near-certain evidence of a scout reading the bait. honeytoken_use (50) means a minted fake credential such as mrg_live_9f2ab04c1d7e83a5c60214bd appeared in an Authorization header, body or query — near-certain evidence, and it names exactly which decoy leaked. path_enumeration (25) fires on the eighth distinct unknown path inside 60 seconds; unknown excludes /, protected routes, scanner paths, decoys and lead paths. Medium class — request shape. ua_suspicious (15): a UA containing sqlmap/, nikto, nuclei, python-requests/ and the rest of data/ua-suspicious.txt. ua_rotation (20): four or more distinct non-empty UAs in five minutes. no_cookie_persistence (15): a fifth request in a session that has never sent a Cookie header and was spotless until now. headers_sparse (10) and ua_missing (10): requests with fewer than four headers or no user agent at all — real browsers send neither shape.

sections.heading: The gating rules (normative)
sections.text: Three signals are gated to prevent the classic false positives. Each rule is exercised by golden vectors. curl gating. tooling_curl fires only when a same-request signal fired earlier in evaluation order — that is, one of signals 1–5. headers_sparse does NOT ungate it, and prior session score does NOT ungate it. Rationale: curl/ appears in legitimate API checks and health probes. ua_rotation gating. Requires ≥ 4 distinct UAs in the trailing 300 s AND another same-request signal from the ungating set (signals 1–5). A session that merely rotates UAs — some privacy tools do — is never scored on rotation alone. no_cookie_persistence gating. Fires only in an otherwise-clean session: request count ≥ 5 (including the current request), never a cookie, cumulative score 0 before, and no other signal this request. It never stacks with scanner or decoy evidence — those already explain the session. A weight tie for reason_code resolves to the earliest signal in evaluation order (vector v17: scanner_path over path_enumeration, both 25). What the fired signals add up to is the verdict ladder. Verified bots, owner IPs and other never-scored addresses produce no signals at all — see modes and the charter for why that is deliberate.

pages.title: Verdicts
pages.description: The Mirage verdict ladder with exact thresholds, the request-vs-cumulative score arithmetic, the protected-route cap and worked numeric examples.

sections.text: Every request gets exactly one verdict. The rungs, lowest to highest: observe < tag < decoy_route < throttle < ban The verdict is the highest rung whose condition holds — computed from the request's own score and class, never from gut feeling, and never from anything a model guessed.

sections.heading: The score arithmetic
sections.text: request_score = sum of the weights of the signals that fired this request. request_class = the highest class among them (high if any high-class signal fired). cum_before = the session's cumulative score before this request. The event records score = cumulative after this request (cum_before + request_score). Rung Condition Action observe No rung below holds pass tag request_score ≥ 15 OR cum_before ≥ 25 pass decoy_route request_score ≥ 25 AND class high AND the path is decoyable (matches a decoy entry; not protected) serve_decoy throttle request_score ≥ 40 adapter-local throttle ban honeytoken_use fired, OR (decoy_lead_follow fired AND path not protected), OR (request_score ≥ 60 AND class high) short block, only when enforcement is enabled (I9) The ladder below stacks the five rungs with their exact thresholds, and the two annotations mark the rules that bound how high a verdict can climb: the protected-route cap and the history rule. {% include diagrams/verdict-ladder.html %}

sections.heading: What history can and cannot do
sections.text: Session history can tag; it can never escalate past tag. A clean-looking request in a dirty session with cum_before ≥ 25 gets tag — recorded, passed, nothing more. decoy_route, throttle and ban are decided by the request's own score and class alone. A session cannot be throttled or banned by accumulation (vector v16: after cumulative 50, a spotless request tags and passes).

sections.heading: The protected-route cap (I4)
sections.text: On a protected route the verdict is capped at tag — login, checkout and API prefixes are never decoyed or throttled by decoy logic. One exception: honeytoken_use survives the cap and produces ban. A leaked fake credential in use is near-certain evidence regardless of route (vector v05: POST /api/v1/auth with the minted bearer token → ban on a protected path).

sections.heading: Ban parameters and renewal
sections.text: A ban covers a single address for 1,800,000 ms (30 minutes), with reason code = the highest-weight signal of the banning request; a weight tie resolves to the earliest signal in evaluation order. Bans are always reversible (I5). While a ban is active (protect mode, enforcement armed), any request from the address renews it: the decision cites the ORIGINAL reason code and the remaining TTL, with request score 0 and no signals — a banned address must not earn its way out with clean-looking requests. Flipping the kill switch disarms renewal within one decision (I9).

sections.heading: Worked examples
sections.text: W1 — scanner path, plain browser. GET /.env, browser UA, 8 headers. Fires scanner_path 25 (high); decoy_hit is suppressed. Tag rung holds (25 ≥ 15); decoy_route holds (25 ≥ 25, high, decoyable); throttle does not (25 < 40). Verdict: decoy_route, recorded score 25 (vector v02). Scanner path plus curl — check the gate before you add. GET /.env with UA curl/8.5.0 and a full header set. The naive sum is scanner_path 25 + tooling_curl 15 = 40, but tooling_curl is gated: it fires only when a signal from the ungating set (signals 1–5) fired earlier in the same request. scanner_path is signal 1 and did fire, so the gate opens and both count: 25 + 15 = 40, class high. Rungs: tag (40 ≥ 15), decoy_route would hold on /.env (40 ≥ 25, high, decoyable) but throttle outranks it (40 ≥ 40), ban does not (40 < 60, no near-certain signal). Verdict: throttle. Contrast vector v10 request 1: GET /products with curl/ and 3 headers fires only headers_sparse 10 — headers_sparse does not ungate tooling_curl — so the request scores 10 and stays observe. The gate, not the weight table, decides what fires. W3 — scanner path plus attack-tool UA. GET /.env, UA sqlmap/1.8: scanner_path 25 + ua_suspicious 15 = 40 → throttle (vector v09, request 2; cumulative 55 recorded). W2 — protected route. GET /wp-login.php, UA sqlmap/1.8: ua_suspicious 15 → tag; the protected path caps at tag anyway. Structure-only ceiling. Seven scripted requests (empty UA, 2 headers, distinct unknown paths) each score 20 → tag; the eighth distinct unknown path adds path_enumeration 25 → request 45 → throttle, never ban: no near-certain signal fired and 45 < 60 (vector v06, W5 — I5 in action). A ban from a combination requires 60 with high class: vector v17 reaches 70 (scanner_path 25 + path_enumeration 25 + headers_sparse 10 + ua_missing 10) → ban. The signals themselves are specified in signals; what each mode does with a verdict is the modes ladder.

pages.title: Decoys
pages.description: The Mirage decoy catalog: personas, entries, leads and honeytokens, how serving works, render determinism, and writing your own entry.

sections.text: Decoys are Mirage's answers to scouts: inert, consistent fake surfaces served only to sessions already scored suspicious. The catalog is data, not code — one YAML file shared verbatim by the Go core and the TypeScript worker (generated into src/generated/ at worker build time), specified by spec/DECOY-CATALOG.md v1.

sections.heading: Catalog structure
sections.text: A catalog has personas and entries. A persona is one consistent fake identity — stack, headers, error style, file layout all agree, because inconsistency is how an attacker spots a trap. v1 ships three personas (laravel-staging, legacy-cpanel, node-api-dev) and six entries: id persona path env-file-staging laravel-staging /.env git-config-staging laravel-staging /.git/config admin-panel-legacy legacy-cpanel /admin/login debug-endpoint-legacy legacy-cpanel /debug api-docs-dev node-api-dev /api/docs source-map-dev node-api-dev /app.js.map Each entry carries a status, content_type, extra headers, size_cap_bytes, a body template, leads and honeytokens.

sections.heading: Leads and honeytokens
sections.text: Both are traps inside a served decoy, at different depths: A lead is a path that exists only inside a decoy response — the log file named in the fake .env, the /admin/login/verify action of the fake panel. Following one fires decoy_lead_follow (40, high); on an unprotected path that is a ban. Leads are registered for a session only when that decoy is served to it. A honeytoken is inert credential material minted into the body per session. The token_alnum_24 format is deterministic: "mrg_live_" + hex(sha256(session_key + ":" + entry_id + ":" + token_id)):24 — the first 24 hex characters of the digest, so a token names its session, entry and slot without a database. Using the exact string anywhere Mirage can see (Authorization header, body keys, query) fires honeytoken_use (50, high) and proves which decoy leaked. Every format lives in the mrg_ namespace that no real service issues, or uses reserved hosts (I14); formats are catalogued in data/token-formats.md.

sections.heading: When a decoy is served
sections.text: Only on a decoy_route verdict — never on tag, throttle or ban, which record and act but do not serve. look mode caps every verdict at tag, so no decoy is ever served there; tripwires and protect serve. Protected routes are never decoyed (I4), verified bots and ordinary visitors never see a decoy (I12), and every response carries X-Robots-Tag: noindex, nofollow, noarchive regardless of template headers, plus robots.txt disallow and absence from sitemaps.

sections.heading: Render determinism
sections.text: Bodies are templates with {{SEED:}} and {{TOKEN:}} slots. Seeds derive from sha256(session_key + ":" + entry_id + ":seed:" + spec + ":" + k), where k counts occurrences of that spec string in the body — two identical slots never render the same value, and the derivation is byte-identical across the Go and TypeScript engines. Formats: {{SEED:N_HEX}} (first N hex chars, N ≤ 64), {{SEED:N_B64}} (N unpadded base64 chars, N a multiple of 4), {{SEED:N_UPPER}} (N digest bytes folded mod 36 over A-Z0-9). The rendered body of every entry for two fixed session keys is pinned byte-for-byte by spec/golden-vectors/renders.json; both engines must reproduce it exactly, and CI fails on any divergence.

sections.heading: The pollution suite
sections.text: Every decoy change runs it (I12–I15): crawl the test site as a verified search bot and assert zero decoy URLs and zero hidden links; assert the noindex header set on every decoy response; run secret scanners and format validators over the rendered catalog to prove no live-valid credential patterns, real personal data or real domains; assert depth, size and connection caps under load; and a feed-poisoning test proving forged reports produce no ban.

sections.heading: Writing your own entry
sections.text: Entries are YAML and the lowest-barrier contribution. A realistic addition to the shipped catalog: The rules the catalog loader enforces at load time: entry paths are unique within the catalog, and a lead must not claim /.well-known/ or collide with an entry path (ids must be unique too). Staying off real routes, robots.txt, sitemaps and health checks is catalog-author discipline — the shipped catalog complies — and the engine independently caps protected routes at tag, so a colliding entry is never served there (I4). Beyond the paths: bodies are inert — no scripts, no redirects, no third-party links (I8, I14); hostnames come from reserved namespaces only (example.com, .test, .invalid, the RFC 5737 ranges); no real brands beyond technology-stack markers; no prose content, only technical artifacts (I13). Validate with go test ./internal/decoy/ — changes to the shipped catalog also update the render fixture, and both engines' suites must stay green. Serving rules are decided by the verdicts ladder; audience rules by modes.

pages.title: Modes
pages.description: The three Mirage modes — look, tripwires, protect — as an operational ladder, with the kill switch, the enforcement opt-in and what each mode does.

sections.text: Mirage is observe-by-default (I9): enforcement exists only when the owner turns it on, twice. The three modes are a ladder — each rung is useful alone, moving up is a one-line config change, and moving down is deleting that line. The mode never changes what the engine measures; it changes what Mirage does about it.

sections.heading: The ladder
sections.text: look (default). Observe and record only. Every verdict is capped at tag — the rung is honest about what the adapter may do, so no decoy is named and no TTL is proposed — and the action is always pass. Signals, scores and reason codes survive the cap: the event keeps the evidence (I10). No decoy is served, nothing is enforced. tripwires. Everything look records, plus decoys: a decoy_route verdict keeps its serve_decoy action — the decoys ARE the tripwires — while throttle and ban verdicts stay recorded with their actions passing. Real traffic is untouched, and decoys still never reach verified bots or ordinary visitors (I12). protect. Enforcement becomes possible — and only possible. It runs only when enforcement.enabled: true (a separate opt-in; enabling it in any other mode is a boot-time error), the kill switch is off, and the budgets are not exhausted. Mode protect alone turns nothing on. Without the opt-in block — or with the kill switch engaged — decisions disarm to the tripwires action set: decoys still serve, throttle and ban actions pass.

sections.heading: What you see versus what Mirage does
sections.text: look tripwires protect (not armed) protect (armed) Verdicts recorded yes, capped at tag all all all Decoys served no on decoy_route on decoy_route on decoy_route Throttle executed no no no yes Bans executed no no no yes, budget-capped Connector calls no no no on ban and reconcile Dashboard full full full full The verdict ladder itself is specified in verdicts and never changes with mode.

sections.heading: The kill switch
sections.text: enforcement.kill_switch: true stops everything at once: no ban or throttle is executed, no connector is called, the system drops to observe. It is re-checked on every decision, so flipping it takes effect immediately — including on renewal: an existing ban stops answering on the address's next request, rather than after a full TTL. Flip it when anything looks wrong; investigate afterwards.

sections.heading: Budgets
sections.text: Protect mode is budget-capped (I5, I15). Defaults: at most 10 bans per minute, at most 100 concurrent bans, at most 5% of sessions banned. When a budget is exceeded, enforcement drops to observe rather than over-ban — under-enforcing during a deliberate flood is the accepted trade; a bug that bans the world is worse than an attacker who returns. Never-ban ranges (owner IPs, loopback, RFC 1918, CGNAT 100.64.0.0/10, link-local) are never banned whatever the engine says.

sections.heading: The dashboard token
sections.text: The dashboard requires a token even on loopback — an unauthenticated local endpoint is one curl away from a full takeover. An empty dashboard_token is a boot-time error, not advice. Generate with openssl rand -hex 32.

sections.heading: Choosing a rung
sections.text: Start at look and read the dashboard until the event stream makes sense. Move to tripwires when you want scouts answered with inert decoys. Move to protect only after reading known limits and the operations runbook — and with the kill switch within reach. The dashboard copy follows the same rule as this documentation: it says "watching", not "protected", unless protect is actually on.

pages.title: Tooling
pages.description: Every quality gate and lab in the Mirage repo: the Makefile targets, the golden-vector generator, the fault-injection matrix and the docs-site gates.

sections.text: Mirage's tooling is deterministic on purpose: agents and humans propose code, the gates decide. Everything CI runs is runnable locally with make check. No Go gate needs network access; the two worker targets do (npm ci).

sections.heading: Makefile targets
sections.text: Target What it runs help Print the target list (the default target). fmt gofmt, rewriting every Go file in place. fmt-check Fail (exit 1) if any Go file is not gofmt-clean. vet go vet ./.... build go build ./... — the library core. test go test -race ./... — every test under the race detector. vectors python3 tools/gen_vectors.py — regenerate the golden vectors and cross-check both sources. worker-build In packages/mirage-worker: npm ci && npm run build (needs network). worker-test In packages/mirage-worker: npm ci && npm test (needs network). slop Grep gate over .go, .ts, .mjs, .sh and the Makefile: word-boundary, case-sensitive matches for unfinished-work markers fail the build; the decoy-template slot word is allowed only in the renderers that own it. spec/, docs/ and data/ are not code and are never scanned. check fmt-check vet build test vectors slop — every gate CI runs. clean Remove build and test artifacts; never touches mirage.db or dotfiles.

sections.heading: The golden-vector generator
sections.text: tools/gen_vectors.py (Python 3, needs PyYAML) is two sources of truth that cross-check each other: hand-computed expectations written out in each case's notes, and an independent reference engine implementing spec/SIGNALS.md v1.1.0. Run from the repo root it regenerates spec/golden-vectors/vectors.json and HAND-COMPUTED.md — and exits 1, printing every mismatch, if the two hands disagree. No vector is emitted that both have not agreed on. The catalog is loaded from the real spec/decoy-catalog/catalog.yaml so the vectors can never drift from it. See testing for adding a case.

sections.heading: The fault-injection lab
sections.text: lab/faultinject proves the fail-open invariants hold when everything around the decision path is broken. Each scenario builds a real stack — real rules, real catalog, real engine, queue, gatekeeper, dashboard, config through the real loader — and injects exactly one fault family, asserting system behavior (exact verdicts, actions, bounded timings), never just "it did not crash": Scenario Fault Proves store-down Every store method fails I1, I3, I10 queue-flood Queue at capacity 100, drainer never started I3, I10 connector-dead Connector Apply always errors I1, I5, I10 connector-hang Connector Apply blocks until released I1, I3, I5 budget-exhausted MaxBansPerMinute 1, two ban-grade attackers I5, I9, I10 never-ban Ban-grade replay from an owner range I6, I15 deadline-overrun Decision clock jumps past the budget I1, I3 kill-switch Boot with the switch on; then a live flip I9, I10 dashboard-storm 50 concurrent workers, mixed tokens, broken store I1, I7, I11 Run it: Exit 0 only when every selected scenario passed; failures are named on stderr. An unknown -only name is a usage error listing the valid names.

sections.heading: The worker build
sections.text: packages/mirage-worker builds in three steps, failing on the first error: scripts/gen-data.mjs regenerates src/generated/data.ts from the shared repo data files and catalog (deterministic output, no timestamps, so regeneration produces a diff only if the shared data really changed); then tsc --project tsconfig.json type-checks; then tsc --project tsconfig.build.json emits dist/ as multi-file ES2022 modules — no bundler, Cloudflare bundles the ESM graph itself. npm test (vitest) replays the full shared golden-vector corpus plus the cross-engine render fixture and the handler suite. Never hand-edit the generated snapshot.

sections.heading: The docs-site gates
sections.text: Two scripts guard this site. tools/sync_site_docs.py keeps the docs/ mirrors of spec/ and data/ fresh — run it after changing a spec or a shared data file, and run it with --check in CI to fail when mirrors are stale. tools/check_site.py validates the site itself: front matter on every page, internal links, navigation entries, and consistency between llms.txt and docs.json. Both exit non-zero on any finding; a gate that cannot run cleanly fails, it never passes silently. The full test architecture — what each suite pins, and how to extend the vectors — continues in testing.

pages.title: Operations
pages.description: The Mirage production runbook: choosing a store, budget tuning, connector selection, dashboard usage, ban renewal and fail-open behavior.

sections.text: This is the runbook for running Mirage on real traffic. The mode ladder and its safety rails are covered in modes; this page is about the knobs underneath.

sections.heading: Choosing a store
sections.text: SQLite in WAL mode is the default (store.path, default mirage.db): one file, safe concurrent reads, events and ban records survive a restart, kept for store.retention_days (default 30, bound 1–3650). The in-memory store is for tests and ephemeral deployments — a restart loses events, while decisions stay correct (the engine's session snapshot is in memory in every configuration). store.hash_ips: true (default) stores salted-hashed client IPs; an explicit false is honored and trades privacy for debuggability.

sections.heading: Budgets
sections.text: Budget Default Effect when exceeded Decision budget 5 ms The decision degrades to fail-open pass; the adapter never waits. Event queue 10,000 events (bound 100–1,000,000) The newest event is dropped and counted in /api/status (queue.dropped). Bans per minute 10 Enforcement drops to observe; verdicts still record. Concurrent bans 100 Same. Share of sessions banned 5% (bound 1–100) Same. The ban budgets exist so Mirage can never ban its way through legitimate traffic (I5, I15). Raising them is a deliberate risk decision, not tuning.

sections.heading: Choosing connectors
sections.text: Connectors deliver bans (and unbans) — only in protect mode, only when armed. All are optional; protect without connectors is a valid local-enforcement deployment. Connector Pick it when Notes denyfile You run nginx/Apache on the same host. Zero dependencies; atomic rewrites (temp file, fsync, rename), one line per address, sorted; the reload is yours to automate. webhook You want bans in your own automation. POSTs JSON signed with hex HMAC-SHA256 in X-Mirage-Signature; verify before acting. crowdsec You already run CrowdSec. Pushes to the local LAPI as alerts with one decision, origin mirage. cloudflare Your zone is on Cloudflare. Zone IP access rules, mirage: -prefixed for ownership; anything un-prefixed is never touched. No connector credential lives in the config file (I11): each block carries only the NAME of an environment variable (api_key_env, api_token_env, secret_env), resolved at call time and never stored on the Config. A missed or crashed Apply heals on the reconcile pass (every 30 s), which also removes stale and revoked bans from providers.

sections.heading: Dashboard usage
sections.text: The dashboard is a separate server from the proxy: it binds --dashboard-addr (default 127.0.0.1:8090, loopback only — non- loopback binds are refused) and requires the token even on loopback. Reach it through an SSH tunnel, not a public bind: Endpoints: /healthz (tokenless probe, fixed body), /api/status (mode, spec and protocol versions, uptime, queue length and drops, store health, connector health), /api/events (recorded decisions), /api/sessions (per-session summaries), /api/bans (ban records) and POST /api/bans/revoke — the one-click reversal every ban must have (I5). Listing endpoints page with a limit parameter (default 50, capped at 1,000). Every response is JSON with Cache-Control: no-store.

sections.heading: Renewal, reversal and the kill switch
sections.text: An active ban renews on every request from the banned address, citing the original reason and remaining TTL — long bans do not silently expire under sustained probing. Reversal is POST /api/bans/revoke (the reconcile loop removes it from providers within 30 s). The kill switch disarms renewal within one decision. Session state itself expires after 30 idle minutes, starting a fresh epoch with cumulative score 0.

sections.heading: Upgrade discipline
sections.text: Run make check before every deploy — the same gates CI runs (tooling). Config loading is strict and fails closed at boot: unknown keys, out-of-bound values and half-configured connector blocks are boot-time errors, so a bad config stops the process, not the site. Validate staged changes with mirage doctor --config mirage.yaml (exit 0 / 1).

sections.heading: What fail-open means operationally
sections.text: A broken Mirage is an invisible Mirage (I1). Store down: decisions stay exact, event persistence fails loudly in logs, /healthz stays 200. Queue full: events drop and count; requests never wait. Connector dead or hung: the local ban holds, the request returns promptly, reconcile heals later. Decision overruns the budget: the request passes unscored. The one deployment rule that follows: keep the origin reachable directly, so removing Mirage from the path is a one-line edit, not an architecture change — the nginx topology shows the break-glass pattern.

pages.title: Testing
pages.description: How Mirage is tested: golden vectors, the race suite, the pollution suite, the fault matrix, worker parity, and how to add a new vector.

sections.text: Mirage's test architecture exists to make one claim checkable: two implementations, written twice, produce identical decisions. Every layer below pins a piece of that claim, and the tooling page lists the commands.

sections.heading: Golden vectors
sections.text: spec/golden-vectors/vectors.json is the executable contract: 20 cases, 68 requests, each with hand-computed expectations — signals, verdict, score, reason code. spec/golden-vectors/HAND-COMPUTED.md shows the arithmetic for every case, written out from spec/SIGNALS.md v1.1.0. The expectations are cross-checked by an independent reference engine inside tools/gen_vectors.py, which refuses to emit on any disagreement (exit 1, mismatches printed). Both the Go suites (internal/detect, internal/service) and the worker suite (packages/mirage-worker/test/engine.vectors.test.ts) replay the same file; CI fails on any divergence. The vectors use only reserved values — RFC 5737 client IPs, RFC 2606 hostnames (I14).

sections.heading: The suites around them
sections.text: Race suite — go test -race ./... covers the engine, queue, store, gatekeeper, connectors and service under concurrency. Pollution suite — internal/decoy asserts the web stays clean: verified-bot crawls see zero decoy URLs, every decoy response carries the noindex set, secret scanners and format validators find no live-valid credentials, and bodies stay inert (I12–I14). Fault matrix — lab/faultinject builds real stacks and breaks one thing at a time (store, queue, connector, budget, deadline, kill switch, dashboard) asserting exact behavior, not survival. Render parity — spec/golden-vectors/renders.json pins the rendered body of every catalog entry for two fixed session keys, consumed by both internal/decoy/render_golden_test.go and the worker's test/render.golden.test.ts. Worker handler suite — vitest covers the fail-open paths (engine throw, budget overrun), the local action responses, the event ring bounds and request translation.

sections.heading: How to add a vector
sections.text: The vectors are generated, never hand-edited: vectors.json and HAND-COMPUTED.md are both emitted by the generator. To add a case: Write the case with its hand computation. In tools/gen_vectors.py, add a case(...) to CASES: an id, a reserved client IP (192.0.2.0/24, 198.51.100.0/24 or 203.0.113.0/24), a note that writes out the arithmetic per HAND-COMPUTED.md style, the requests (the R helper) and the expectations (the E helper). Compute every expectation by hand from spec/SIGNALS.md — the note is the proof. Run the cross-check. make vectors runs the generator; if your hand computation and the reference engine disagree, it exits 1 and names the field. Fix one of them — usually the hand computation — before anything else. A case whose auth hint needs a minted honeytoken resolves it at generation time, the way the existing cases do. Run the consumers. go test ./internal/detect/ and go test ./internal/service/ must replay the new case green; then cd packages/mirage-worker && npm test must do the same in TypeScript. CI runs all of this via make check plus make worker-test. Record canon decisions. If your case pins a previously ambiguous rule, add it to the canon-decisions list the generator writes at the end of HAND-COMPUTED.md, the way the existing entries do. If the case exposes a spec disagreement rather than an implementation bug, the spec changes first — bump spec_version, regenerate the vectors, and let every suite fail until both engines agree again. That spec-first rule is the discipline that keeps two implementations honest. The FAQ answers the questions this architecture raises most often.

pages.title: FAQ
pages.description: Twelve honest answers about Mirage: why no ML, WAF replacement, CGNAT handling, false positives, licensing, performance and limits.

sections.text: These answers follow the claims policy: every claim links to something reproducible, and the honest form of "stops attack agents" is "detects scouting and wastes attacker effort". What Mirage cannot do is written down first in known limits.

sections.heading: Why is there no machine learning?
sections.text: Because determinism is the product. A rule-based engine is explainable, replayable and auditable: every verdict traces to signals, weights and a reason code, and the same request always scores the same (I10, pinned by the golden vectors). The cost is stated openly: rule-based means rule-gapped — novel reconnaissance patterns need new rules.

sections.heading: Is Mirage a WAF replacement?
sections.text: No. Decoys catch scouting, not exploits: an attacker who goes straight for a real vulnerability touches no decoy and is not slowed down. Mirage sits beside a WAF and answers a different question — who is mapping the site — and enforcement is opt-in, budget-capped and reversible (I5, I9).

sections.heading: What about carrier-grade NAT and mobile networks?
sections.text: Shared and CGNAT ranges (100.64.0.0/10) are never banned, along with loopback, link-local, private ranges, owner IPs and CDN ranges (I15). Bans are single-address by design; an attacker behind rotating infrastructure comes back, which is the accepted price of never banning an innocent shared address.

sections.heading: What is the false-positive posture?
sections.text: Weights are chosen so benign single-fire requests stay under the tag threshold of 15: headers_sparse (10) alone observes, and the three classic false positives are gated out — tooling_curl needs same-request evidence, ua_rotation never fires on rotation alone, and no_cookie_persistence only fires in an otherwise-spotless session. Verified bots and owner ranges are never scored at all.

sections.heading: What does the license split mean for me?
sections.text: The Go core is AGPL-3.0; adapters, SDKs and the Cloudflare Worker are Apache-2.0, so the edge pieces can be embedded anywhere permissive licensing requires. Self-hosting Mirage does not require publishing anything; if you distribute a modified core, AGPL's source obligations apply — read LICENSE and packages/mirage-worker/LICENSE, not this FAQ, before deciding.

sections.heading: Is this Cloudflare-only?
sections.text: No. The worker is one adapter; the Go core runs anywhere behind any TLS-terminating proxy — the nginx topology is the reference — and both implement one spec with identical verdicts.

sections.heading: What is the performance envelope?
sections.text: Decisions run against an in-memory snapshot under a hard 5 ms budget, with no network call, disk wait or LLM call in the request path (I3). On any internal failure or budget overrun the request passes to the origin unscored (I1) — Mirage degrades before it delays.

sections.heading: Where does my data live?
sections.text: Locally. Events, sessions and ban records go to the store you configure (default SQLite in WAL mode); connectors make outbound calls only, and there is no phone-home — telemetry is off by default and stays off unless you opt in.

sections.heading: Can attackers detect Mirage?
sections.text: Over time, any fixed decoy set can be fingerprinted and skipped — stated in known limits (community decoy packs are planned after 1.0; none ship today). Decoys carry no public "this is a decoy" marker (ADR-0001): safety comes from audience gating, noindex headers and a published security.txt contact for legitimate researchers.

sections.heading: What happens when the store dies?
sections.text: Traffic continues and decisions stay exact (I1): the store-down fault scenario proves the ladder answers identically with every store method failing. Event persistence fails loudly in logs; /healthz stays 200; nothing blocks.

sections.heading: Why 30-minute bans?
sections.text: Short, reversible, budget-capped bans are the invariant (I5, I15): a default ban covers a single address for minutes to hours, never a range, with a recorded reason and a one-click undo. The TTL is configurable (enforcement.ban_ttl_ms), but the shape — earned, short, reversible — is not negotiable.

sections.heading: Can I just stay in look mode forever?
sections.text: Yes. Every rung is useful alone; look mode is a complete product — the dashboard, the event stream and the reason texts. Moving up is a config change; moving down is deleting one line.

pages.description: The Mirage reference shelf: every configuration key, every CLI subcommand, the shared data files, and the normative specs.

sections.text: The reference pages are complete enumerations, not tutorials. Each one walks its source file key by key or command by command, so a claim made anywhere else in this documentation can be checked here against the exact default, bound or flag. If a number on a guide page and a number here ever disagree, this page and the file it mirrors are wrong together with it — file that as a bug. Page What it enumerates Configuration Every key of mirage.example.yaml — type, default, validation bound, what it controls, and the invariant behind it. CLI The mirage subcommands: serve, doctor, init, posture, replay, version — flags, exit codes and --json shapes.

sections.text: Policy lives in data/, shared verbatim by the Go core and the TypeScript worker (the worker's build regenerates its snapshot from these files, so the two engines can never drift): File Contents data/scanner-paths.txt The scanner path list behind scanner_path (SIG-101). data/ua-suspicious.txt Attack-tool user-agent substrings behind ua_suspicious (SIG-106). data/ua-verified-bots.txt Verified-bot hints; a match marks the request never-scored. data/reserved-hosts.txt Reserved hostnames and ranges permitted in decoy content (I14). data/token-formats.md The inert honeytoken formats (the mrg_ namespace). data/reason-texts.txt Plain-English renderings for every reason and verdict code (I10).

sections.heading: The spec library
sections.text: The normative documents every implementation must satisfy. Changes bump the recorded version and regenerate the golden vectors: Spec Version Governs spec/SIGNALS.md 1.1.0 The 11 signals, weights, classes, gating, the verdict ladder, session semantics. spec/ADAPTER-PROTOCOL.md 1 The DecisionRequest / Decision / Event contract, deadlines, fail-open, conformance. spec/DECOY-CATALOG.md 1 The catalog format, personas, template slots, honeytoken formats, the pollution suite. spec/golden-vectors/ — The executable contract: 20 cases / 68 requests, plus the render fixture. For prose that explains rather than enumerates, start at the guide index. For machine-readable consumption of this documentation, see Reading Mirage as an agent.

pages.title: Configuration Reference
pages.description: Every key of the Mirage site config with its type, default, validation bound, what it controls, and the invariant behind it.

sections.text: This page walks mirage.example.yaml key by key — the complete annotated config surface, which mirrors internal/config exactly. Loading is strict: a YAML file must decode with KnownFields enabled, so a typo or an unknown key is a boot-time error, never a silently disabled security control. config.Validate lists ALL violations before failing; Mirage fails closed at boot and open at request time (I1).

sections.heading: Identity and network
sections.text: Key Type Default Bound / validation Controls Why mode string "look" One of look, tripwires, protect; anything else is rejected at boot The integration ladder (see modes) I9: observe by default; enforcement needs more than the mode site string "" Free text Site name or origin URL used in dashboards and reports Identification only listen string "127.0.0.1:8080" Valid address The address the proxy binds Loopback by default; the dashboard never binds listen — it is a separate loopback server on --dashboard-addr trusted_proxies list of CIDR none (socket address only) Every entry must parse as a CIDR or boot fails Proxies whose X-Forwarded-For chain is trusted; walked right-to-left, the first non-trusted address is the client I6: an unlisted peer's forwarding headers are ignored entirely, so an attacker cannot frame an innocent address. List ONLY proxies you control dashboard_token string required Must not be empty — a hard validation rule, not advice The token guarding every dashboard endpoint except /healthz An unauthenticated local endpoint is one curl away from a takeover. Generate with openssl rand -hex 32. The one secret carried inline; the loader ships Redacted() for safe logging (I11) owner_ips list of CIDR none Every entry must parse as a CIDR Ranges that are never scored and never banned (office egress, VPN, load balancer) I6, I15: requests from them produce verdict observe and record no session state protected_routes list of strings the five routes below A route ending in / is a prefix match; anything else matches exactly Routes never decoyed and never throttle-capped by decoy logic I4. Absent means the canon default; an explicitly empty list () means no protected routes — a deliberate choice made out loud Canon protected_routes default: /wp-login.php, /wp-admin/, /checkout, /cart, /api/.

sections.text: Key Type Default Bound / validation Controls Why events.queue_capacity int 10000 100..1000000 Capacity of the bounded event queue between the request path and the store I3: when the queue is full the newest entry is dropped and counted — emission never blocks a request

sections.text: All connector blocks are optional. A block left entirely empty counts as not configured; setting any key of a block requires its siblings — half-configured connectors are boot-time errors. No connector credential lives in this file (I11): each block carries only the NAME of an environment variable holding the secret; the value is resolved at call time and never stored on the Config.
