sections.heading: Loading rules worth remembering
sections.text: Copy the example to mirage.yaml (gitignored on purpose) — or generate one with mirage init, which writes mode: "look" and a generated dashboard_token (nothing else) and validates the file before reporting success. The decoy-path rules — duplicate entry paths, leads under /.well-known/, lead/entry collisions — are enforced by the catalog loader at load time (I4), not by init. Every violation is listed before the boot fails, so one edit can fix them all. Validate staged changes without booting: mirage doctor --config mirage.yaml (see the CLI reference). The operations guide explains how to choose between these values; this page only states what they are.

pages.title: CLI Reference
pages.description: The mirage CLI: serve, doctor, init, posture, replay and version, with flags, exit codes and the --json output shapes.

sections.text: The mirage binary has six subcommands. --config FILE names the site config on every subcommand that takes one — required on serve, doctor, posture and replay (no default), and the file to write on init (default mirage.yaml); version takes no flags. Exit codes are uniform: 0 success, 1 failure or mismatch — the same convention as the repo's quality gates, so scripts can trust a single check.

sections.heading: mirage serve
sections.text: Runs the core: loads and validates the config (strict — a bad config exits 1 before serving anything), then runs two servers. The proxy binds listen, scores every request that reaches it, forwards traffic to the upstream, serves decoys per mode and drives enforcement and connectors. The token-guarded dashboard binds its own loopback address (/healthz, /api/status, /api/events, /api/sessions, /api/bans, POST /api/bans/revoke). Any internal failure during a decision answers pass to the request (I1). Flag Default Meaning --config FILE required Site configuration file --upstream URL required Upstream origin URL the proxy forwards to — there is no upstream key in the config --listen ADDR the config's listen (127.0.0.1:8080) Proxy listen address --dashboard-addr ADDR 127.0.0.1:8090 Dashboard listen address — loopback only, non-loopback binds are refused

sections.heading: mirage doctor
sections.text: Validates a config file without serving: strict decoding, every policy bound, the dashboard-token requirement, mode/enforcement consistency, connector completeness. Human output lists each check; --json emits the machine form. Shape: The check names are real for a default config; the detail strings are illustrative. The shape is exact: ok, mode, spec_version, and checks of {name, ok, detail}. ok is true only when every check passed; the process exits 0 on ok, 1 otherwise. (The JSON block above shows the shape of the envelope — field values are illustrative.) Flag Default Meaning --config FILE required Site configuration file --json false Emit machine-readable JSON instead of the check table

sections.heading: mirage init
sections.text: Writes a minimal valid config — mode: "look" and a crypto/rand dashboard_token are the only keys; every other key keeps its documented default — and loads the written file back through strict validation before reporting success. Init checks nothing else: the decoy-path rules are the catalog loader's, enforced when a catalog is loaded, not at install time. Exits 1 if the target exists (unless --force) or the generated file fails validation. Flag Default Meaning --config FILE mirage.yaml Configuration file to write --force false Overwrite an existing file

sections.heading: mirage posture
sections.text: Reviews the site's effective posture from its config: mode, enforcement state, budgets, protected routes and connector readiness. --json emits {"mode", "warnings", "checks": {"name", "value"}} — there is no ok key: any config that loads and validates exits 0, and warnings are advisory. Use it before moving up the mode ladder — it answers "what would this config actually do" without booting the server. Flag Default Meaning --config FILE required Site configuration file --json false Emit machine-readable JSON instead of the report

sections.heading: mirage replay
sections.text: Replays a vector file through the real engine and config, comparing every expected field (signals, verdict, score, reason code) the way the test suites do. Exit 0 only on full parity; exit 1 names the first mismatch and counts the rest. --json emits {"ok", "total", "passed", "failed", "cases"} — one entry per case with its first divergence. This is the command for verifying a modified config or catalog against the executable contract before deploying. Flag Default Meaning --config FILE required Site configuration file --vectors PATH spec/golden-vectors/vectors.json Golden vector file to replay --json false Emit machine-readable JSON instead of the per-case lines

sections.heading: mirage version
sections.text: Prints the build version; it accepts no flags. The decision protocol the build speaks is version 1 and the signal spec is 1.1.0 — the same versions carried in every Decision, so a deployed binary can be matched to its spec revision.

sections.heading: Notes for scripting
sections.text: --json exists on doctor, posture and replay only; serve logs, init writes a file, version prints one line. --config is required on serve, doctor, posture and replay; on init it selects the file to write (default mirage.yaml); version accepts none. An unknown flag or subcommand is an error (exit 1), matching the fail-closed-at-boot discipline of the config loader. Machine consumers should read the agent page for the full machine-readable surface.

pages.title: Signal Specification
pages.description: SIGNALS v1.1.0 — the eleven signals, fixed weights and classes, gating rules, evaluation order and the verdict ladder.

sections.text: Normative. Every implementation (Go core, TypeScript worker) must produce identical results on spec/golden-vectors/vectors.json. CI fails on any divergence. Changes to this file bump spec_version and regenerate vectors. spec_version: "1.1.0"

sections.heading: 1. Scope and inputs
sections.text: The engine scores one HTTP request at a time, deterministically, against an in-memory session snapshot. It never calls the network, disk or an LLM (I3). Inputs per request: Field Type Notes method string GET/HEAD/POST/... path string Raw path including dot segments and query string client_ip string Socket address or trusted-proxy result (see §2) user_agent string Header value, may be empty or absent header_count int Count of ALL request headers, including Host and User-Agent has_cookie bool A Cookie header is present and non-empty ts_ms int64 Request time, milliseconds since epoch auth_hint string Optional: credential material visible to the adapter (query, Authorization header, body keys), matched against known honeytokens Adapters that cannot see a field pass the neutral value and the engine degrades gracefully: signals requiring the field do not fire.

sections.heading: 2. Client identity
sections.text: Session key = first 32 hex characters of sha256(client_ip). Example: sha256("203.0.113.7"):32 = fec52565aa0cf18f57d7cf5b3ac72850. Client IP comes from the socket address, or from X-Forwarded-For / related headers only when the immediate peer is a trusted proxy listed in config. The chain is walked right-to-left, skipping trusted proxies; the first non-trusted address is the client. Untrusted peers' forwarding headers are ignored entirely — an attacker must not be able to frame an innocent address (I6). Never-scored addresses (verified in data/reserved-hosts.txt and config): owner IPs, loopback, CDN and load-balancer ranges, allowlisted bots — no dashboard-token exception exists (the token authenticates dashboard endpoints, it does not switch scoring back on). Requests from them produce verdict observe and no session state is recorded. Verified bot hints: a case-insensitive user-agent substring match against data/ua-verified-bots.txt marks the request never-scored. The Go core additionally supports reverse-DNS plus forward confirmation for Googlebot when the owner enables it; the hint list is the hot-path gate.

sections.heading: 3. Path handling
sections.text: Strip the query string (everything from the first ?). Normalize dot segments: resolve . and .. left to right, popping the previous segment. .. at the root pops nothing — the path is clamped at / and the request is marked dot_escape (it signals scanner-style path fuzzing). Matching against scanner, decoy and protected lists is exact on the normalized path. Catalog loader normalization: a scanner-list entry with a trailing slash also matches the entry without it (/phpmyadmin-old/ matches /phpmyadmin-old).

sections.heading: 4. Signals
sections.text: Weight, class and reason code are fixed. high classes can escalate; medium classes alone can never ban (I5). # id weight class reason fires when 1 scanner_path 25 high SIG-101 Normalized path matches data/scanner-paths.txt or dot_escape fired 2 decoy_hit 30 high SIG-102 Normalized path matches a decoy catalog entry. Suppressed when scanner_path fired the same request (a scanner-list hit is already fully explained) 3 decoy_lead_follow 40 high SIG-103 Normalized path matches a lead path that exists only inside a decoy response served earlier to this session 4 honeytoken_use 50 high SIG-104 Any credential material visible in the request matches a honeytoken minted for a decoy served to this session 5 path_enumeration 25 high SIG-105 ≥ 8 distinct unknown paths in the trailing 60 s window. Unknown = not /, not a protected route, not a scanner path, not a decoy, not a decoy lead 6 ua_suspicious 15 medium SIG-106 User-Agent matches data/ua-suspicious.txt (case-insensitive substring) 7 ua_rotation 20 medium SIG-107 ≥ 4 distinct non-empty user agents from the session in the trailing 300 s AND at least one other signal fired this request (gated, §6) 8 no_cookie_persistence 15 medium SIG-108 Request count ≥ 5 for the session, no Cookie header ever in the session, session cumulative score was 0 before this request, and no signal earlier in evaluation order fired (gated, §6) 9 headers_sparse 10 medium SIG-109 header_count < 4. Fires on every sparse request 10 ua_missing 10 medium SIG-110 User-Agent header absent or empty string 11 tooling_curl 15 medium SIG-111 User-Agent matches curl/ AND at least one of scanner_path, decoy_hit, decoy_lead_follow, honeytoken_use, path_enumeration fired this request earlier in evaluation order (gated, §6) Evaluation order is the table order 1→11. A signal later in the order may read, but never change, the outcome of an earlier one.

sections.heading: 5. Verdict ladder
sections.text: Rungs, lowest to highest: observe < tag < decoy_route < throttle < ban. Let request_score = sum of weights of signals that fired this request. Let request_class = the highest class among them. Let cum_before = session cumulative score before this request. Let path_protected = normalized path is a protected route (I4). tag: request_score ≥ 15 OR cum_before ≥ 25. decoy_route: request_score ≥ 25 AND request_class = high AND the path is decoyable (matches a decoy entry; not protected). throttle: request_score ≥ 40. ban: honeytoken_use fired, OR (decoy_lead_follow fired AND path is not protected), OR (request_score ≥ 60 AND request_class = high). The verdict is the highest rung whose condition holds. Protected-route cap (I4): on a protected path the verdict is capped at tag, with one exception — honeytoken_use survives the cap and produces ban (R3 exception: a leaked fake credential in use is near-certain evidence regardless of route). Ban parameters: single address, TTL 30 minutes, reason code = the highest-weight signal of the request. Always reversible (I5).

sections.heading: 6. Gating rules (normative)
sections.text: These prevent the classic false positives. Each is exercised by vectors. curl gating. tooling_curl fires only when a same-request signal fired earlier in evaluation order (signals 1–5). headers_sparse does NOT ungate it. Prior session score does NOT ungate it. Rationale: curl/ appears in legitimate API checks and health probes. ua_rotation gating. Requires ≥ 4 distinct user agents in the trailing 300 s AND a signal from 1–5 in the same request. A session that merely rotates UAs (some privacy tools do) is never scored on rotation alone. no_cookie_persistence gating. Fires only in an otherwise-clean session (request count ≥ 5, never a cookie, cumulative score 0 before, no signal earlier in evaluation order this request; signals later in the order — headers_sparse, ua_missing, tooling_curl — may co-fire). Never stacks with scanner or decoy evidence — those already explain the session.

sections.heading: 7. Session state and expiry
sections.text: State per session key: first_ts, last_ts, request_count, cumulative_score, cookie_ever (bool), ua_seen (list of (ua, ts)), unknown_paths (list of (path, ts)), decoys_served (list of decoy ids), leads_known (lead paths from served decoys), tokens_minted (honeytoken strings from served decoys). Expiry: if ts - last_ts > 30 × 60 × 1000 ms (30 minutes), the state resets before scoring — a new session epoch begins, cumulative score 0. Windows (ua_seen, unknown_paths) keep only entries inside their trailing window (300 s / 60 s) after every request. Recorded score: the event records score = cumulative score AFTER this request (cum_before + request_score). The verdict rung uses only the request's own score and class (§5). History alone never escalates: a clean-looking request in a dirty session can tag (via cum_before ≥ 25) but never throttles or bans on history alone.

sections.heading: 8. Output
sections.text: reason_code = the highest-weight signal of the request; ban_ttl_ms is set only on ban verdicts (1800000). Plain-English renderings for every reason code live in data/reason-texts.txt and must be used by every dashboard and report (I10). All attacker-controlled strings are untrusted input at render time (I7).

sections.heading: 9. Reserved test values
sections.text: Vectors use only reserved values (I14): client IPs from 192.0.2.0/24, 198.51.100.0/24, 203.0.113.0/24 (RFC 5737); hostnames from example.com / .test / .invalid (RFC 2606). No real brands in decoy content beyond technology-stack markers permitted by the decoy catalog spec.

sections.heading: 10. Worked examples
sections.text: These are normative and mirrored in the golden vectors. W1 — scanner path, plain browser UA. GET /.env, UA Mozilla/5.0 (X11; Linux x86_64), 8 headers, cookie present. Fires scanner_path 25 (high). decoy_hit suppressed (§4.2). Verdict: decoy_route (25 ≥ 25, high, decoyable). Recorded score 25. W2 — protected route, tool UA. GET /wp-login.php, UA sqlmap/1.8. Fires ua_suspicious 15. Request score 15 → tag; protected path caps at tag anyway. Recorded score 15. W3 — scanner path plus tool UA. GET /.env, UA sqlmap/1.8. Fires scanner_path 25 + ua_suspicious 15 = 40 → throttle (40 ≥ 40). W4 — honeytoken on a protected route. POST /api/v1/auth with Authorization: Bearer mrg_live_ where the token was minted in the /.env decoy served earlier to this session. Fires honeytoken_use 50 → ban, surviving the protected-route cap (§5). W5 — structure-only session. Seven scripted requests (empty UA, 2 headers, distinct unknown paths, no cookie): each fires headers_sparse 10 ua_missing 10 → tag (20 ≥ 15). The eighth distinct unknown path within 60 s fires path_enumeration 25 too → request score 45 → throttle. Never ban: no high-class near-certain signal (I5).

pages.title: Adapter Protocol
pages.description: The v1 contract between an edge adapter and Mirage Core: the request, the decision, the action set and the event.

sections.text: Normative. Every edge adapter (Go middleware, Cloudflare Worker, future plugins) speaks this protocol. A conformance suite runs against each adapter before it ships; golden-vector parity is mandatory. protocol_version: "1"

sections.heading: 1. Shape
sections.text: An adapter is a synchronous decision point plus an asynchronous event emit: Two transports are allowed (I3): In-process: the engine is a library linked into the adapter (Go middleware, Worker bundle). Decision is a function call. Local IPC: unix socket or loopback HTTP to a local Mirage Edge process, with a hard deadline. No remote calls in the hot path.

sections.heading: 2. DecisionRequest
sections.text: client_ip is the adapter's best client IP after its own trusted-proxy walk. trusted_peer says whether the immediate peer was a trusted proxy. deadline_ms is the maximum wall-clock budget the adapter will wait. Recommended: 5 ms. On overrun the engine returns the fail-open decision.

sections.heading: 3. Decision
sections.text: action ∈ pass | serve_decoy | throttle | ban: pass — forward to origin unmodified (observe, tag). serve_decoy — the adapter renders the decoy identified by decoy_id from its local snapshot. Never a network fetch (I3, I2). throttle — apply the adapter's local throttle (e.g. 429 or tarpit with caps); the origin is protected but never hard-failed by Mirage itself. ban — the adapter blocks (short TTL) only if enforcement is enabled for the site; otherwise it degrades to throttle. Enforcement is opt-in (I9). The fail-open decision — returned on any internal error, unknown protocol version, or deadline overrun — is always: Reason code SIG-000 is reserved for fail-open and is never a ban input.

sections.heading: 4. Event
sections.text: Emission is asynchronous and bounded: a ring buffer with a configured cap (default 10 000 events). When full, oldest events are dropped and a drop counter increments. Emitting must never block the hot path. Events are idempotent by (session_key, ts_ms, path); consumers must tolerate replays after Core recovery. All fields are attacker-influenced: consumers escape on render (I7).

sections.heading: 5. Conformance requirements
sections.text: An adapter is conformant when: Fail-open proof: with the engine removed, slow, or erroring, 100% of requests reach the origin unmodified within the latency budget. Vector parity: identical verdicts on spec/golden-vectors/vectors.json. Deadline honored: p99 decision overhead < deadline; overrun ⇒ fail-open decision, counter incremented. No asset-path dependency: real routes render identically without Mirage present (I2). Decoy hygiene: decoys served only on serve_decoy; every decoy response carries the noindex header set (I12); no third-party redirects (I8, I14). Event discipline: bounded queue, drop counter, no hot-path blocking.

sections.heading: 6. Versioning
sections.text: protocol_version changes only on breaking wire changes; spec_version tracks the signal spec independently. An adapter that receives a request or snapshot with a newer spec_version than it knows fails open and reports a version-mismatch counter.

pages.title: Decoy Catalog
pages.description: The v1 decoy catalog format: personas, entries, leads, tokens, reserved values and validation rules.

sections.text: Normative format for spec/decoy-catalog/ entries. The catalog is data, not code: shared verbatim by the Go core and the TypeScript worker (generated into src/generated/ at build time by scripts/gen-data.mjs). catalog_version: "1"

sections.heading: 2. Personas
sections.text: A persona is one consistent fake identity per attacker session: stack, headers, error pages, file contents, timestamps and fake IDs all agree, because inconsistency is how an agent or its operator spots a trap. Seeded generation (session key as seed) keeps each session deterministic and reproducible. v1 ships three personas: persona stack story tells laravel-staging Laravel 10 on PHP 8.2 behind nginx, staging environment X-Powered-By: PHP/8.2.12, .env layout, laravel-style logs legacy-cpanel aged shared-hosting cPanel box .cpanel-style paths, Apache-ish headers, old backup listings node-api-dev Node API left in dev mode JSON error payloads, /api/docs, source maps

sections.heading: 3. v1 catalog entries (6)
sections.text: id persona path lures env-file-staging laravel-staging /.env env-file hunters git-config-staging laravel-staging /.git/config git-directory readers admin-panel-legacy legacy-cpanel /admin/login panel seekers debug-endpoint-legacy legacy-cpanel /debug debug-endpoint probers api-docs-dev node-api-dev /api/docs API enumerators source-map-dev node-api-dev /app.js.map source-map miners Catalog safety rules (validated by internal/decoy and mirrored in the worker): Entry paths are unique within the catalog, and a lead must not claim /.well-known/ or collide with an entry path — the catalog loader enforces those at load time (internal/decoy). Entries must also stay off real routes, robots.txt, sitemaps and health checks; that part is catalog-author discipline (the shipped catalog complies), and the engine independently caps protected routes at tag, so a colliding entry is never served there (I4). 2. /.env and /.git/config also appear in data/scanner-paths.txt; the engine suppresses decoy_hit behind scanner_path (SIGNALS §4.2) — the catalog entry is still what gets served on decoy_route. 3. Body templates are inert: no executable content, no scripts, no third-party links, no redirects (I8, I14). 4. Every response carries X-Robots-Tag: noindex, nofollow, noarchive (I12) regardless of template headers.

sections.heading: 4. Placeholders and seeding
sections.text: Placeholders are resolved per session deterministically from sha256(session_key + ":" + entry_id + ":seed:" + spec + ":" + k) where k is the 0-based occurrence index of that spec string in the body — two identical {{SEED:…}} placeholders in one body never render the same value, while the derivation stays byte-identical across the Go and TypeScript implementations. The formula is pinned byte-for-byte by spec/golden-vectors/renders.json (rendered body of every entry for two fixed session keys); both engines must reproduce it exactly. {{SEED:N_HEX}} — first N hex chars of the digest (N ≤ 64). {{SEED:N_B64}} — N unpadded standard-base64 chars (N must be a multiple of 4, derived from the first 3N/4 digest bytes). {{SEED:N_UPPER}} — first N digest bytes folded mod 36 over A-Z0-9. {{TOKEN:id}} — mint the honeytoken for (session, entry, id) as "mrg_live_" + hex(sha256(session_key + ":" + entry_id + ":" + token_id)):24 — the first 24 hex characters of the digest, so a token names its session, entry and slot without a database. The one mintable format is token_alnum_24 in data/token-formats.md. Later use of the exact string anywhere Mirage can see fires honeytoken_use (SIG-104) and proves which decoy leaked. Timestamps inside bodies render from ts_ms of the serving request, so decoys never contradict themselves within a session.

sections.heading: 5. Honeytoken formats (I14)
sections.text: All formats are in the mrg_ namespace that no real service issues, or use reserved hosts/ranges — see data/token-formats.md. A honeytoken must never validate against a real service. The validation suite runs secret scanners over every rendered decoy to prove it.

sections.heading: 6. Pollution suite (pass 7b, runs on every decoy change)
sections.text: Crawl the test site as a verified search bot: zero decoy URLs, zero hidden links. Every decoy response carries the noindex header set; none appear in sitemaps. Secret scanners + format validators over the rendered catalog: no live-valid credential patterns, no real personal data, no real domains outside the permitted technology-stack markers. Depth, size and tarpit connection caps hold under load. Feed-poisoning test: forged reports produce no ban (I15).

pages.title: Golden Vectors — Hand Computed
pages.description: The arithmetic behind all 20 golden vector cases, computed by hand and cross-checked by tools/gen_vectors.py.

sections.text: Spec 1.1.0, protocol 1, 20 cases, 68 requests. Every expectation below is hand-computed from spec/SIGNALS.md and cross-checked by the reference engine in tools/gen_vectors.py; the generator exits 1 on any disagreement. All client IPs are RFC 5737 documentation addresses; all hostnames in payloads are RFC 2606 reserved.

sections.heading: v01-clean-browsing — 203.0.113.20
sections.text: Five ordinary browser requests with cookies and a full header set. No signal can fire: paths are real or harmless unknowns (only 4 distinct unknowns, below the enumeration threshold of 8), headers are full, a cookie is sent, the UA is a browser. Verdicts observe, cumulative 0. # request signals verdict score 1 GET / — observe 0 2 GET /about — observe 0 3 GET /pricing — observe 0 4 GET /blog — observe 0 5 GET /contact — observe 0

sections.heading: v02-scanner-path — 203.0.113.7
sections.text: Worked example W1. GET /.env with a plain browser UA: scanner_path 25 (high); decoy_hit is suppressed by SIGNALS 4.2. request 25 >= 25 with high class on a decoyable path -> decoy_route. Cumulative 25. Session key is the sha256 anchor: fec52565aa0cf18f57d7cf5b3ac72850. # request signals verdict score 1 GET /.env scanner_path decoy_route 25

sections.heading: v03-decoy-hit — 203.0.113.8
sections.text: GET /admin/login (admin-panel-legacy decoy, not on the scanner list). decoy_hit 30, high, decoyable -> decoy_route. Cumulative 30. # request signals verdict score 1 GET /admin/login decoy_hit decoy_route 30

sections.heading: v04-decoy-lead-follow — 203.0.113.9
sections.text: req1: GET /.env -> scanner_path 25 -> decoy_route; the decoy is served, so its lead /storage/logs/laravel-staging.log becomes known to the session. req2 follows the lead: decoy_lead_follow 40 (near-certain), path not protected -> ban. Cumulative 25 + 40 = 65. # request signals verdict score 1 GET /.env scanner_path decoy_route 25 2 GET /storage/logs/laravel-staging.log decoy_lead_follow ban 65

sections.heading: v05-honeytoken-protected — 203.0.113.10

Cumulative 25 + 50 = 75. # request signals verdict score 1 GET /.env scanner_path decoy_route 25 2 POST /api/v1/auth honeytoken_use ban 75

Cumulative after req7: 6 x 20 = 120. req8 (/nope7): distinct unknown paths in the trailing 60 s reach 8 (/products + /nope1-7) -> path_enumeration 25 joins: request 25 + 10 + 10 = 45 -> throttle, cumulative 165. req9 (/nope8): 9 distinct unknowns, same 45 -> throttle, cumulative 210. Never ban: no near-certain signal and request score 45 < 60. # request signals verdict score 1 GET /products — observe 0 2 GET /nope1 headers_sparse, ua_missing tag 20 3 GET /nope2 headers_sparse, ua_missing tag 40 4 GET /nope3 headers_sparse, ua_missing tag 60 5 GET /nope4 headers_sparse, ua_missing tag 80 6 GET /nope5 headers_sparse, ua_missing tag 100 7 GET /nope6 headers_sparse, ua_missing tag 120 8 GET /nope7 path_enumeration, headers_sparse, ua_missing throttle 165 9 GET /nope8 path_enumeration, headers_sparse, ua_missing throttle 210

sections.text: Googlebot UA hits /.env. Verified-bot hint (case-insensitive substring) -> never scored, observe, no session state (I12: bots never meet a trap). # request signals verdict score 1 GET /.env — observe 0

sections.heading: v08-allowlist-ip — 192.0.2.50
sections.text: The owner's own IP (allowlisted in the case config) hits a decoy path. Never scored, observe, no session state. # request signals verdict score 1 GET /admin/login — observe 0

sections.heading: v09-protected-route — 203.0.113.13
sections.text: Worked examples W2/W3. req1: GET /wp-login.php with sqlmap UA (4 headers, above the sparse threshold): ua_suspicious 15 -> tag; the path is protected so the verdict caps at tag anyway. req2: GET /.env with sqlmap UA: scanner_path 25 + ua_suspicious 15 = 40 -> throttle. Cumulative 15 then 55. # request signals verdict score 1 GET /wp-login.php ua_suspicious tag 15 2 GET /.env scanner_path, ua_suspicious throttle 55

sections.heading: v10-curl-gating — 203.0.113.14
sections.text: SIGNALS section 6.1. req1: GET /products with curl UA and 3 headers: headers_sparse 10 fires, but tooling_curl does NOT (no signal from the ungating set 1-5 fired this request; headers_sparse does not ungate). request 10 < 15 -> observe, cumulative 10. req2: GET /.env with curl UA: scanner_path 25 fires first and ungates tooling_curl 15; headers_sparse 10 also fires: 25 + 15 + 10 = 50 -> throttle. Cumulative 60. # request signals verdict score 1 GET /products headers_sparse observe 10 2 GET /.env scanner_path, headers_sparse, tooling_curl throttle 60

sections.heading: v11-ua-rotation-gated — 203.0.113.15
sections.text: SIGNALS section 6.2. reqs 1-4: four distinct non-empty UAs on /products with full headers: at req4 the count reaches 4 but NO other signal fired this request -> ua_rotation must NOT fire (observe). req5: fifth UA on /.env: scanner_path 25 fires and ungates ua_rotation 20 -> 45 -> throttle. Cumulative 45. # request signals verdict score 1 GET /products — observe 0 2 GET /products — observe 0 3 GET /products — observe 0 4 GET /products — observe 0 5 GET /.env scanner_path, ua_rotation throttle 45

sections.heading: v12-no-cookie-persistence — 203.0.113.16
sections.text: SIGNALS section 6.3. Five requests to the same unknown path with a full header set and never a cookie. reqs 1-4: no signal (1 distinct unknown, full headers, normal UA). req5: request count reaches 5, cookie_ever false, cumulative 0 before, no other signal this request -> no_cookie_persistence 15 -> tag. Cumulative 15. # request signals verdict score 1 GET /products — observe 0 2 GET /products — observe 0 3 GET /products — observe 0 4 GET /products — observe 0 5 GET /products no_cookie_persistence tag 15

sections.heading: v13-no-cookie-gated — 203.0.113.17
sections.text: Same as v12, but the fifth request hits /.env. scanner_path fires, so no_cookie_persistence is suppressed (the request is no longer otherwise-clean): only scanner_path 25, high, decoyable -> decoy_route. Cumulative 25. # request signals verdict score 1 GET /products — observe 0 2 GET /products — observe 0 3 GET /products — observe 0 4 GET /products — observe 0 5 GET /.env scanner_path decoy_route 25

sections.heading: v14-session-expiry — 203.0.113.18
sections.text: SIGNALS section 7. req1: GET /.env -> scanner_path 25 -> decoy_route, cumulative 25. req2 arrives 31 minutes later (1 860 000 ms > 30 min TTL): the session resets first, so a clean GET /about is observe with cumulative 0. req3: GET /.env one second later in the fresh epoch: scanner_path 25 -> decoy_route, cumulative 25. # request signals verdict score 1 GET /.env scanner_path decoy_route 25 2 GET /about — observe 0 3 GET /.env scanner_path decoy_route 25

sections.heading: v15-normalization — 203.0.113.19
sections.text: SIGNALS section 3. req1: /shop/../wp-config.php.bak?debug=1 -> query stripped, /shop/.. pops shop -> /wp-config.php.bak, a scanner path -> scanner_path 25. The path is NOT a catalog decoy, so the decoy_route rung does not hold -> tag. req2: /../../.env clamps at the root and resolves to /.env -> scanner_path 25, decoyable -> decoy_route. req3: /a/../../.. pops 'a', then '..' at the root clamps (dot_escape) -> scanner_path fires per 4.1; resolved path / is not decoyable -> tag. Cumulative 25, 50, 75. # request signals verdict score 1 GET /shop/../wp-config.php.bak?debug=1 scanner_path tag 25 2 GET /../../.env scanner_path decoy_route 50 3 GET /a/../../.. scanner_path tag 75

sections.heading: v16-ua-rotation-plus — 203.0.113.21
sections.text: Rotation gate plus history-tagging. reqs 1-3: three distinct UAs on /products, full headers -> observe (3 < 4; rotation must NOT fire at req3). req4: fourth distinct UA, but no other signal this request -> rotation still NOT fired -> observe. req5: GET /admin/login with a fifth UA: decoy_hit 30 ungates ua_rotation 20 -> 50 -> throttle (cumulative 50). req6: clean request, but cumulative 50 >= 25 -> tag via history (verdict rungs use the request's own score except the tag rung, SIGNALS section 5.1). req7: 2 headers -> headers_sparse 10; rotation stays gated (headers_sparse is not in the ungating set 1-5): request 10, tag via history. Cumulative 60. # request signals verdict score 1 GET /products — observe 0 2 GET /products — observe 0 3 GET /products — observe 0 4 GET /products — observe 0 5 GET /admin/login decoy_hit, ua_rotation throttle 50 6 GET /products — tag 50 7 GET /products headers_sparse tag 60

sections.heading: v17-combination-ban — 203.0.113.22
sections.text: Ban through a strong combination (SIGNALS section 5.4c) without any near-certain signal. reqs 1-7: scripted GETs /u1../u7, empty UA, 2 headers: 20 each -> tag, cumulative 140. req8: /u8 -> 8 distinct unknown paths in 60 s -> path_enumeration 25 + 10 + 10 = 45 -> throttle, cumulative 185. req9: GET /.env: scanner_path 25 + path_enumeration 25 (unknowns u1-u8 still in window) + headers_sparse 10 + ua_missing 10 = 70 >= 60 with high class -> BAN. Cumulative 255. # request signals verdict score 1 GET /u1 headers_sparse, ua_missing tag 20 2 GET /u2 headers_sparse, ua_missing tag 40 3 GET /u3 headers_sparse, ua_missing tag 60 4 GET /u4 headers_sparse, ua_missing tag 80 5 GET /u5 headers_sparse, ua_missing tag 100 6 GET /u6 headers_sparse, ua_missing tag 120 7 GET /u7 headers_sparse, ua_missing tag 140 8 GET /u8 path_enumeration, headers_sparse, ua_missing throttle 185 9 GET /.env scanner_path, path_enumeration, headers_sparse, ua_missing ban 255

sections.heading: v18-query-and-slash — 203.0.113.23
sections.text: req1: GET /.env?token=abc123 -> the query is stripped before matching -> scanner_path 25 -> decoy_route. req2: GET /phpmyadmin-old -> loader normalization (SIGNALS 3.3): the list entry /phpmyadmin-old/ matches the slashless path -> scanner_path 25; not a decoy -> tag. Cumulative 25, 50. # request signals verdict score 1 GET /.env?token=abc123 scanner_path decoy_route 25 2 GET /phpmyadmin-old scanner_path tag 50

sections.heading: v19-honeytoken-reuse — 203.0.113.24
sections.text: req1: GET /.env -> decoy_route; the env decoy mints db_password. req2 uses the minted token inside a fake postgres URL carried as credential material on /api/v2/users (protected): honeytoken_use 50 -> ban despite the cap. Cumulative 75. # request signals verdict score 1 GET /.env scanner_path decoy_route 25 2 POST /api/v2/users honeytoken_use ban 75

sections.heading: v20-ip-spoof-rejected — 198.51.100.5
sections.text: Invariant I6. The request carries X-Forwarded-For: 203.0.113.99, but the peer is not a trusted proxy, so the client IP stays the socket address 198.51.100.5 and the session key is sha256('198.51.100.5'):32 = 8959edf6884f2c2e223a9319e83a6982. The attacker cannot frame the innocent 203.0.113.99. Clean request -> observe. # request signals verdict score 1 GET /about — observe 0

sections.heading: Canon decisions (recorded to keep implementations honest)
sections.text: The ungating set for tooling_curl and ua_rotation is signals 1-5 (scanner_path, decoy_hit, decoy_lead_follow, honeytoken_use, path_enumeration). headers_sparse and other medium signals never ungate (mirrors SIGNALS 6.1 for curl; applied consistently to rotation). no_cookie_persistence gates on signals 1-7 (its predecessors in evaluation order); headers_sparse / ua_missing / tooling_curl may co-fire with it. A weight tie for reason_code resolves to the earliest signal in evaluation order (e.g. v17 req9: scanner_path over path_enumeration, both 25). Unknown-path counting for enumeration excludes ALL catalog lead paths (not only served ones); a lead is Mirage's territory. request_count for the no-cookie gate includes the current request (fires on the 5th at the earliest). Decoy serving (and therefore lead registration and honeytoken minting) happens only on verdict decoy_route; throttle and ban do not serve.

pages.title: Quickstart
pages.description: The shortest honest path to a running Mirage: build, check, configure, watch the first decisions.

sections.text: This page is the honest path from a fresh clone to a working Mirage installation: build, verify, configure, serve, and watch the first decisions.

sections.heading: Status: what runs today
sections.text: Shipped and tested: the components listed in this section, each behind the repo's gates — nothing has been released yet, and the changelog tracks the work under Unreleased. The normative specs and golden vectors; the Go core (config, model, store, events, enforce, connectors); the SIGNALS v1.1.0 detection engine; the decoy data layer; the in-process HTTP edge middleware (internal/edge); the mirage CLI — serve, doctor, init, posture, replay, version (cmd/mirage); the fault-injection lab; and the Cloudflare Worker port. Every gate runs in CI on every push: make check (fmt, vet, build, race tests, golden-vector cross-check, slop scan), the worker's npm build + test suite, and the docs-site gates. Run the Go core in front of an upstream with mirage serve --upstream …, or put the Cloudflare Worker at the edge — same signals, same vectors, same verdicts.

sections.heading: What you need
sections.text: git and GNU make. Go 1.23 or newer — the module pins go 1.23.0 (see go.mod; the repo builds with the go1.23.4 toolchain). Python 3 with PyYAML — only for the golden-vector gate (tools/gen_vectors.py imports yaml). pip install pyyaml if you lack it. Node 20 or newer and npm — only for the worker package (packages/mirage-worker/package.json requires node >=20).

sections.heading: 2. Verify everything (the same gates CI runs)
sections.text: That runs, in order: fmt-check (gofmt-clean tree), vet (go vet ./...), build (go build ./...), test (go test -race ./...), vectors (regenerate the golden vectors and cross-check the two independent sources in tools/gen_vectors.py; the generator exits 1 on any disagreement), and slop (the unfinished-work-marker grep gate). make help lists every target. If make check is green, you have the same evidence the CI workflow produces on main — that is the claim: deterministic gates, not trust. The build emits bin/mirage (via make build, with the version and commit stamped in), the Go core under internal/, and the edge middleware — the full self-hosted surface plus the worker port.

sections.heading: 3. Create your config and the dashboard token
sections.text: Or hand-write it from the annotated surface: Open mirage.yaml and make two decisions: dashboard_token — replace the CHANGE-ME marker with the value you just generated. The dashboard requires a token even on loopback (an unauthenticated local endpoint is one curl away from a takeover). This is the one secret that lives in the config file; connector secrets live only in environment variables. mode — start at look. The three modes are documented inline in the example file: look observes and records only, tripwires additionally serves inert decoys to sessions already scored suspicious, protect additionally makes enforcement possible (it still needs enforcement.enabled: true, the kill switch off, and the budgets in range — I9). Every key, default, bound and rule in that file mirrors internal/config/config.go exactly; loading is strict (unknown keys and half-configured connector blocks are boot-time errors), so a typo can never silently disable a security control.

sections.heading: 4. Run it (self-hosted)
sections.text: The proxy forwards everything to --upstream; with no origin of your own yet, give it a demo one in a second terminal: serve composes the whole stack — store, engine, catalog, queue, gatekeeper, connectors — into the edge middleware: benign traffic proxies through to the upstream, scanner paths are answered with persona decoys (from tripwires mode up), and the token-guarded dashboard listens on loopback at --dashboard-addr (default 127.0.0.1:8090; non-loopback binds are refused). A realistic first session: Note that requests from loopback are never scored (I6, I15) — exercise the decision path from a real address. mirage replay re-runs the golden vectors through the full composed service any time you want proof the arithmetic still holds. The reverse-proxy topology in front of serve — TLS termination, X-Forwarded-For, trusted_proxies, the deny map — is documented in nginx.md.

sections.heading: 5. Run it at the edge (Cloudflare)
sections.text: If your site is behind Cloudflare, the worker carries the same detection engine, the same decoy catalog snapshot and the same golden-vector parity, in-process, with no runtime dependencies: The full walkthrough (wrangler.toml, routes, the reserved MIRAGE_TOKENS binding, how the shared catalog data is regenerated, fail-open semantics) is in cloudflare-worker.md. Both shapes implement one spec and produce identical verdicts on the shared golden vectors — deploy the worker at the edge, the self-hosted core at the origin, or both.

sections.heading: 6. Upgrading modes later
sections.text: Mode upgrades are a one-line config change; downgrades are deleting that line. From look, move to tripwires when you want scouts to be answered with inert decoys (never to verified bots or ordinary visitors — I12). Move to protect only after reviewing the enforcement limits in known-limits.md: bans are single-address, short and budget-capped (I5, I15), Tor and VPN exits are tagged rather than banned, and when a budget is exceeded Mirage drops to observe rather than over-ban. enforcement.kill_switch: true stops all enforcement instantly from anywhere on the ladder.

sections.text: nginx.md — transparent-proxy integration, the deny map. cloudflare-worker.md — the edge deployment. reference/cli.md — every subcommand, flag and exit code. vendor-notes.md — CrowdSec, Cloudflare and the webhook receiver contract. SECURITY.md — how to report a vulnerability and what mrg_ honeytokens are.

pages.title: nginx Topology
pages.description: Run Mirage as a transparent proxy behind nginx: X-Forwarded-For handling, trusted proxies, the deny map and the fail-open contract.

sections.text: This is the reference topology for self-hosted Mirage: nginx terminates TLS and proxies to Mirage; Mirage scores each request, serves decoys to already-suspicious sessions, and passes everything else to your origin unmodified. Everything on this page is runnable today — the mirage serve binary is shipped — and nothing is hypothetical about Mirage's side: every behavior described is pinned by internal/config (the listen and trusted_proxies keys), internal/service (the proxy and the loopback dashboard), internal/connectors (the deny map and webhook connectors) and the invariants.

sections.heading: What Mirage needs in front
sections.text: A TLS-terminating proxy. Mirage does no TLS termination in v1 — it sits behind nginx (or Caddy, or Cloudflare). This keeps Mirage's attack surface small; see known-limits.md. One proxy hop it can trust. Mirage derives the real client IP from the socket address, or from X-Forwarded-For only when the immediate peer is a trusted proxy listed in trusted_proxies (I6). The chain is walked right-to-left, skipping trusted proxies; the first non-trusted address is the client. A peer that is not listed has its forwarding headers ignored entirely — an attacker must not be able to frame an innocent address by sending a forged X-Forwarded-For. An origin that stays reachable. Mirage never sits between your users and your site as the only path: any internal failure sends traffic to the origin unmodified (I1). nginx keeps the origin as the fallback — see the fail-open section below.

sections.heading: The worked configuration
sections.text: nginx side — terminate TLS, forward everything to Mirage's listen address (default 127.0.0.1:8080, from listen in mirage.yaml): Mirage side — mirage.yaml: Do not add addresses you do not control to trusted_proxies. A listed proxy can spoof client identity to Mirage; an unlisted one cannot.

sections.heading: The loopback dashboard
sections.text: The dashboard is a separate server from the proxy: it binds --dashboard-addr (default 127.0.0.1:8090), loopback only — non- loopback binds are refused at startup — while the proxy itself binds listen. Reach the dashboard through an SSH tunnel instead of opening it: The dashboard requires a token even on loopback — an unauthenticated local endpoint is one curl away from a full takeover. Generate it with openssl rand -hex 32 and set dashboard_token in mirage.yaml. This is a hard validation rule, not advice: an empty token is a boot-time error.

sections.heading: The deny map
sections.text: The denyfile connector (internal/connectors/denyfile.go) maintains an nginx-compatible deny map: one line per address, sorted, and written atomically — content goes to a temp file in the same directory, is fsynced, then renamed over the target, so a crash mid-rewrite leaves the previous map intact rather than a truncated include your web server would refuse to load (I1). Configure it with connectors.denyfile.path (for example /etc/nginx/mirage-deny.conf) and include it in the location block as shown above. The file looks like this: nginx picks up deny-map changes only on reload. Mirage writes the file; it does not signal nginx — an automated reload belongs to your automation. The natural place is a small webhook receiver: Mirage signs every ban and unban notice with X-Mirage-Signature (vendor-notes.md documents the exact verification), and your receiver runs nginx -t && nginx -s reload only after the signature checks out.

sections.heading: Mode matrix
sections.text: mode What Mirage does on a request What nginx must do look Observe and record only. No decoys are served, nothing is enforced. Nothing beyond proxy_pass above. tripwires As look, plus: sessions already scored suspicious are served inert decoys on decoy routes. Real routes untouched (I12: never to verified bots or ordinary visitors). Nothing. Decoys are served by Mirage, not by nginx. protect As tripwires, plus enforcement may run — only with enforcement.enabled: true, kill switch off, budgets in range (I9). Optional: include the deny map and automate the reload. Moving between modes is a mirage.yaml edit; each mode is fully reversible.

sections.heading: The fail-open contract (I1)
sections.text: Mirage fails open by design: any internal failure — crash, timeout, bad config, full disk — sends traffic to the origin unmodified. Mirage must never be the reason a site is down. Three practical consequences for this topology: Keep the origin reachable directly. A break-glass location (or a commented proxy_pass pointing at the origin) lets you take Mirage out of the path in one edit. Moving down a rung is deleting one line, not re-architecting. The origin fetch is never Mirage's to retry. In the worker this is pinned by code (origin errors are never mistaken for Mirage errors); the same discipline applies here — an origin outage must surface as an origin outage. The deny map is the only synchronous enforcement surface, and it degrades safely: rewrites are atomic and sorted so the map is always loadable, and Reconcile prunes expired entries so a stale ban cannot outlive its TTL. The file must exist before nginx loads it — create it empty first, or use the glob include shown above, which tolerates absence.

pages.title: Cloudflare Worker
pages.description: Build, configure and deploy the zero-dependency worker port, including secrets and shared-data regeneration.

sections.text: This is the deployment that runs today: a Cloudflare Worker carrying the same SIGNALS v1.1.0 detection engine and decoy catalog as the Go core, in-process, with zero runtime dependencies (the only imports are Mirage's own modules and a build-time-generated data snapshot). The worker is Apache-2.0 (packages/mirage-worker/LICENSE), so it can travel anywhere permissive licensing requires. Every claim below is pinned by code: the build chain in packages/mirage-worker/scripts/build.mjs and scripts/gen-data.mjs, the handler in src/worker.ts, and the test suites in packages/mirage-worker/test/.

sections.heading: Build
sections.text: npm run build runs three steps, in order, failing on the first error: scripts/gen-data.mjs — regenerates src/generated/data.ts from the shared repo data files and the decoy catalog, so the snapshot in the bundle can never drift from the spec sources. tsc --project tsconfig.json — type-checks src and test (noEmit). tsc --project tsconfig.build.json — emits dist/ as multi-file ES2022 modules. There is deliberately no bundler step: Cloudflare Workers accept multi-file ESM uploads and wrangler deploy bundles the emitted graph itself, so the honest build is plain tsc. The output entry point is dist/worker.js (from src/worker.ts). Run the suite while you are here — it replays the full shared golden-vector corpus (20 cases / 68 requests) against the same engine, plus the cross-engine render fixture:

sections.heading: Deploy
sections.text: There is no wrangler.toml in the repository — configuration is yours. Create one in the package directory, next to the built dist/: compatibility_date must not be in the future for the wrangler version you run. Then, from packages/mirage-worker: wrangler is not a devDependency of the package (it would pull a large tree into the zero-runtime-dependency guarantee); npx wrangler deploy uses the pinned latest wrangler on demand. You need the Cloudflare account to allow your user access to the target zone.

sections.heading: Secrets
sections.text: The worker needs no secrets in v1 — the engine is deterministic, the catalog data rides in the generated snapshot, and enforcement (the credential-bearing half of Mirage) stays in the Go core. The single reserved binding is MIRAGE_TOKENS, held for a future honeytoken-registry integration; it is accepted by the handler but has no effect on any decision today (see the Env interface in src/worker.ts). When it becomes meaningful, set it without code changes: Secrets belong in the Workers secret store, never in code or in wrangler.toml — the same least-privilege rule the Go core enforces by resolving every connector credential from the environment (I11).

sections.heading: Keeping the shared data current
sections.text: The engine's data — scanner paths, suspicious and verified-bot user-agent patterns, reserved hosts, and the decoy catalog — is shared verbatim with the Go core. scripts/gen-data.mjs regenerates the snapshot: Run it from inside the package directory in a full checkout: the script anchors its input paths at the package root and reads ../../data/scanner-paths.txt, ../../data/ua-suspicious.txt, ../../data/ua-verified-bots.txt, ../../data/reserved-hosts.txt and ../../spec/decoy-catalog/catalog.yaml (DECOY-CATALOG.md v1). The output is deterministic — no timestamps — so regeneration produces spurious diffs only if the shared data really changed. npm run build runs the same script as its first step, and make worker-build from the repo root runs the full chain. Never hand-edit src/generated/data.ts; it is marked GENERATED, and the parity suites fail if the engines ever disagree.

sections.heading: How the worker behaves (and fails)
sections.text: Fail-open is the contract (ADAPTER-PROTOCOL §3, I1), implemented in src/worker.ts: A hard 5 ms decision budget (DECISION_DEADLINE_MS, matching the protocol's recommendation). If scoring and acting overrun it, the request passes to the origin unmodified. Any internal error — engine throw, deadline overrun, decoy render failure — produces the reserved fail-open decision (verdict observe, action pass, reason code SIG-000) and the request still reaches the origin unmodified. The origin fetch stays outside the error boundary, so an origin network error is never mistaken for a Mirage error and never retried by Mirage. Local actions only, when a verdict says so: decoy_route serves the decoy rendered locally from the in-bundle catalog snapshot — never a network fetch, never a redirect (I3, I2, I8); throttle answers 429 with Retry-After: 30 and nothing else; ban answers 403 with a plain body and nothing else. No response header names Mirage or leaks the ban TTL (ADR-0001) — the header set matches the Go edge byte for byte, and remaining TTL is an operator concern that lives in the event stream. Stateless across isolates. Workers share no memory between invocations, so durable bans and throttles belong to the Go core; the worker's ban/throttle are per-request local responses. Long-horizon session signals are therefore approximate in worker mode — a recorded limit in known-limits.md. Client identity comes from CF-Connecting-IP, set by the Cloudflare platform and unspoofable by clients. Spoofable headers like X-Forwarded-For are deliberately never scored (I6). A bounded event ring (10 000 events, oldest dropped) keeps conformance with the adapter protocol's event contract in each isolate, with failOpen and dropped counters exposed for ops probes via getEventStats(). All of the above is exercised by npm test: the handler suite covers the fail-open paths (engine throw, budget overrun), the local action responses, the ring bounds and the request translation, and the engine suite replays the full golden-vector corpus shared with the Go implementation.

pages.title: About
pages.description: What Mirage is, what runs today, and where the repository's honest status line stands — the README, unedited.

sections.text: !ci(https://github.com/namandhakad712/Mirage/actions/workflows/ci.yml) Open-source tripwires and decoys that show you who is scanning your website and waste their time — set up in ten minutes, no security background needed. Mirage detects automated reconnaissance (scanner noise, AI attack agents, opportunistic crawlers) and answers it with inert decoys. It never breaks the site it protects, and it never pollutes the public web. Start here: docs/deploy/quickstart.md — from zero to a verified build, a config with a generated dashboard token, a running mirage serve proxy, or the Cloudflare Worker at the edge. Hosted docs: https://namandhakad712.github.io/Mirage/ — the whole guide, the specs, and a machine-readable surface (/llms.txt, /docs.json) for AI agents.

sections.heading: Install
sections.text: Two honest paths, no install script, nothing touches PATH: Release binaries — v0.1.0 ships static builds (linux amd64/arm64, macOS amd64/arm64, Windows amd64) with SHA-256 checksums. Download, chmod +x, and mirage version prints the stamped build. From source — git clone https://github.com/namandhakad712/Mirage && cd Mirage && make build with a Go 1.23 toolchain emits ./bin/mirage; make check runs every gate CI runs.

sections.heading: What it is
sections.text: Watch — see who knocks: decoy hits, scanner paths, tool signatures. Tripwires — decoy paths (/.env, /.git/config, fake panels, fake source maps) served to suspicious sessions only. Real traffic untouched. Edge scoring — per-request deterministic scoring inside your own edge (Go middleware, or a Cloudflare Worker). Enforce — short, reversible, budget-capped bans through connectors (CrowdSec, Cloudflare, deny-maps), off by default. Each rung is useful alone and fully reversible. Moving up a rung is a config change; moving down is deleting one line.

sections.heading: What it is not
sections.text: It does not stop an attacker who goes straight for a real vulnerability. Decoys catch scouting, not exploits. See Known limits. No hack-back, ever. Passive deception only. No web pollution: decoys are never indexable, never served to verified search engines, never contain misinformation or live credentials. See the Charter. Not a hosted service. Self-hosted, no phone-home, telemetry off by default.

sections.heading: Architecture
sections.text: Two implementations, one spec: the Go core and the TypeScript worker must produce identical verdicts on the shared golden vectors. CI fails on any divergence. Package One line internal/model Shared decision types, session key sha256(ip):32, the right-to-left trusted-proxy client-IP walk (I6), never-scored/never-banned ranges, reason-text sanitizer (I7). internal/config Strict YAML site config: fail-closed unknown-key rejection, every policy bound, the loopback dashboard-token requirement (I9, I11). internal/store SQLite (WAL) and in-memory stores behind one interface; versioned schema with safe migration. internal/events Bounded event queue: when full, the newest event is dropped and counted — emission never blocks the hot path (I3); the worker's ring buffer drops the oldest instead. internal/detect The SIGNALS v1.1.0 decision engine: deterministic scoring, verdict ladder, gating rules; the golden-vector parity target. internal/decoy The decoy data layer: strict catalog loader, reserved-value validation, deterministic renderer, pollution suite (I8, I12–I14). internal/enforce The verdict gatekeeper: per-verdict budgets and the global kill switch (I5, I9). internal/connectors Denyfile, webhook, CrowdSec LAPI and Cloudflare adapters behind one retry envelope (backoff + jitter, 429 Retry-After honored). packages/mirage-worker The Cloudflare Worker: TypeScript port of the engine, zero runtime dependencies, in-process and fail-open (Apache-2.0). Decisions are made on an in-memory snapshot under a hard deadline — no network call, disk wait or LLM call in the request path (I3) — and any internal failure sends the request to the origin unmodified (I1).

sections.heading: The connectors
sections.text: Enforcement is opt-in (I9) and delivered by four connectors, each fail-open by design and fully documented in vendor notes with the exact API surfaces they call: Connector What it does Config keys denyfile Maintains an nginx/Apache-compatible deny map with atomic rewrites. connectors.denyfile.path webhook POSTs ban/unban notices signed with X-Mirage-Signature (hex HMAC-SHA256). connectors.webhook.url, connectors.webhook.secret_env crowdsec Pushes bans to a local CrowdSec LAPI (alerts + decisions, origin mirage). connectors.crowdsec.lapi_url, connectors.crowdsec.api_key_env cloudflare Pushes bans as zone IP access rules, mirage: -prefixed for ownership. connectors.cloudflare.account_id, .zone_id, .api_token_env No connector credential lives in the config file — only the names of the environment variables that hold them (I11). The complete annotated surface, including the mode table and the token rules, is mirage.example.yaml.

sections.heading: The Cloudflare Worker
sections.text: packages/mirage-worker is the deployable piece today: the same detection engine, decoy catalog and golden-vector parity as the Go core, bundled into a zero-runtime-dependency worker that fails open by construction. Deploy it with docs/deploy/cloudflare-worker.md; self-hosted users will proxy through the core instead — see docs/deploy/nginx.md for the transparent-proxy topology.

sections.heading: The constitution
sections.text: Every line of Mirage is checked against fifteen invariants: docs/invariants.md. The first three: Fail-open. Any internal failure sends traffic to the origin unmodified. Never in the asset path. Your pages never depend on Mirage to load. Hot path is local. No network call, disk wait or LLM call while handling a request. Plus: protected routes are never decoyed, bans are earned and reversible, client IPs come only from trusted proxies, attacker data is treated as hostile input, decoys are inert, enforcement is opt-in with a kill switch, every action is explainable, and no internet pollution (I12–I15).

sections.heading: Repository layout
sections.text: Two implementations, one spec — the parity rule and what it gates are described in Architecture above.

sections.heading: Status
sections.text: All components shipped and gated; the first tagged release is v0.1.0 (static binaries + SHA-256 checksums on the releases page). What exists now: The constitution: fifteen invariants, charter, claims policy, known limits, ADRs. The normative specs (SIGNALS v1.1.0, adapter protocol v1, decoy catalog v1), the shared data files, and the golden vectors — 20 cases / 68 requests, hand-computed and machine cross-checked — plus the cross-engine render fixture. The Go core: model, config, store, events, enforce and connectors, race-tested. The decision engine (SIGNALS v1.1.0 in code) and the decoy data layer. The Go edge middleware and the mirage CLI — serve (transparent proxy + loopback dashboard), doctor, init, posture, replay, version, with --json machine output on the reporting commands. The fault-injection lab proving the invariants hold under store, queue, connector, budget, deadline and kill-switch faults. The Cloudflare Worker — deployable today, response-identical to the Go edge on the shared vectors. The build layer: Makefile gates, CI (Go + worker + docs), the full example config, and the hosted documentation site with its sync and integrity tooling. Version 1.0 is defined by exit criteria, not a date — see docs/design/MIRAGE-DESIGN.md section 12. Watch CHANGELOG.md for progress.

sections.text: Go edge middleware (internal/edge): the in-process HTTP adapter — request extraction mirroring the Worker byte for byte (raw path, header count including Host, cookie presence, ClientIPFrom trusted-proxy walk per I6), decision application (pass / serve_decoy with the persona render / 429 + Retry-After: 30 / plain 403), a defensive wall-clock fail-open guard around Decide on top of the service's own budget checks (I1), panic recovery on the decision and decoy paths, and strict response hygiene: zero Mirage-identifying headers, ever (ADR-0001). 15 test groups green under -race, including the mode matrix, the I6 walk table, concurrency, and real-server header-set assertions. Hosted documentation site (GitHub Pages, Actions build with the same Jekyll engine Pages runs natively): a custom design system (dark default light toggle, CSS custom-property tokens, sticky sidebar navigation, right-rail table of contents, copy-button code blocks, verdict-ladder visual, print-safe typography — no frameworks, no plugins, no remote themes), a landing page, the 11-page guide, the reference shelf (complete config key tables, CLI reference), the agent surface, and synced mirrors of the normative specs and data files. Machine-readable documentation surface: /llms.txt (curated index), /llms-full.txt (flattened full text) and /docs.json (structured manifest) — generated deterministically from the navigation and page front matter, never hand-maintained. Site tooling: tools/sync_site_docs.py (regenerates the spec/data mirrors and the machine manifests; --check mode is a CI gate) and tools/check_site.py (structural integrity: front matter, layout references, navigation completeness, every internal link target, Liquid safety, manifest consistency, docs slop scan). make site-sync / make site-check expose both. CI: a docs job (sync gate + integrity gate + the same actions/jekyll-build-pages build the deploy uses) and a pages workflow (gated build, artifact upload, deploy-pages); a deploy failure never takes the previous site release down. Worker response hygiene (ADR-0001 fix): the Worker no longer stamps X-Mirage-Ban-Ttl (it both fingerprinted Mirage and handed attackers the exact retry moment) or Cache-Control: no-store on throttle/ban — its header set now matches the Go edge byte for byte, and the tests assert the absence of any X-Mirage-* header on every action. Deploy guides updated to the shipped reality: the quickstart now walks mirage init/doctor/posture/serve (with the loopback-never-scored caveat), and the README status section reflects the complete system.

sections.heading: Fixed — 2026-11-26 (render-parity round)
sections.text: {{SEED:*}} derivation is now per-spec-string occurrence-counted: the material is sha256(session_key + ":" + entry_id + ":seed:" + spec + ":" + k) where k is the k-th occurrence of that spec in the body, so two identical placeholders never collide while the formula stays identical across engines. Pinned byte-for-byte by the new cross-engine fixture spec/golden-vectors/renders.json (every catalog entry rendered for two fixed sessions), consumed by BOTH the Go suite (internal/decoy/render_golden_test.go) and the worker suite (packages/mirage-worker/test/render.golden.test.ts); CI fails on any divergence. {{SEED:N_UPPER}} alphabet is 36 chars (A-Z0-9) in both engines — the TypeScript renderer previously used 26 letters and produced different bytes from Go for the same session (caught by the golden fixture, fixed before release). {{SEED:N_HEX}} now slices the digest directly (N ≤ 64) and {{SEED:N_B64}} is unpadded standard base64 derived from 3N/4 digest bytes (N must be a multiple of 4), matching Go exactly. Spec canon updated: spec/DECOY-CATALOG.md §4 now states the exact seed material, the three SEED formats and the golden-fixture pin.

pages.title: Charter
pages.description: The mission, the non-goals, and the line Mirage refuses to cross.

sections.text: This charter is the contract between Mirage and its users. It is short on purpose: everything here is enforceable, and everything enforceable is here.

sections.heading: Scope
sections.text: Mirage protects public HTTP and HTTPS services. It does not cover SSH, databases or mail in version 1 (integration with existing SSH honeypots is possible later). A site entirely behind a login or a private network gains less — the scouts rarely reach it. What Mirage does: Detects noisy reconnaissance and automated attack-agent scouting. Wastes attacker effort with inert, consistent decoys. Enforces short, reversible, budget-capped bans when the owner opts in. What Mirage does not do — and will not do: No hack-back. No executing code on attacker machines, no counter- scanning, no retaliation of any kind. Passive deception only. No web pollution. Decoys never reach search indexes, archives, AI-training crawlers or ordinary visitors (I12). We do not feed garbage to content scrapers (I13) — we block or rate-limit them. No live credentials. Honeytokens use formats that cannot validate, or registered canaries owned by the site owner (I14). A decoy must never become someone else's security incident. No overclaiming. We say "detects scouting and wastes attacker effort". We never say "stops attack agents". Decoys do not stop an agent that goes straight to a real vulnerability. Known limits is written first, not after the first critic. No paywalls on safety features. The posture check, look mode, decoys and the dashboard are free forever. Sponsorships and optional paid support may come later; safety does not. No phone-home. Telemetry is off by default and stays off unless the owner opts in.

sections.heading: Decoy marking decision (recorded)
sections.text: Decoys carry no public "this is a decoy" marker — a marker reveals the trap. Instead we rely on audience gating (decoys are served only to sessions already scored suspicious), noindex headers, robots.txt disallow, and a published security.txt contact so legitimate researchers can ask to be allowlisted. See ADR-0001.

sections.heading: Against the alternatives — honestly
sections.text: Hosted router-tied shields: paywalled and closed. Mirage is free and self-hostable. Vendor "AI labyrinths" aimed at scrapers: they feed generated content to crawlers. Mirage targets attack agents and never pollutes the web. CrowdSec: shared IP reputation. Mirage integrates with it (connector), not competes. Proof-of-work bot blockers: complementary; different problem. "Works with" beats "versus".

sections.heading: Contribution rules
sections.text: Contributions that add hack-back, data poisoning, live credential formats, marketing overclaims, or indexable decoys will be declined by charter. Lowest-barrier contributions: decoy packs (YAML, no code), platform recipes, translations, adapters through the SDK.

sections.heading: Governance
sections.text: docs/invariants.md — the constitution (I1–I15). docs/adr/ — decision records; invariant changes need one. docs/claims-policy.md — every claim links to a reproducible test. docs/known-limits.md — what Mirage cannot do, written first. AGPL-3.0 for the core, Apache-2.0 for adapters and SDKs, so adapters can be embedded anywhere.

pages.title: Invariants
pages.description: I1-I15: the properties every line of Mirage must preserve, and the tests that hold them.

sections.text: These fifteen invariants are binding. Every feature, pull request and agent run is checked against them, and at least one test exists for each one. A human maintainer can waive one only through a recorded ADR in docs/adr/.

sections.heading: I1 — Fail-open
sections.text: Any internal failure — crash, timeout, bad config, full disk — sends traffic to the origin unmodified. Mirage must never be the reason a site is down. Test hooks: fault-injection suite (lab/faultinject) kills Core, corrupts config and stalls the store while asserting the pass-through path stays clean.

sections.heading: I2 — Never in the asset path
sections.text: The customer's JavaScript bundle and pages never depend on Mirage to load. This is the key difference from a hosted "serve your bundle through us" mode. Test hooks: adapter conformance suite asserts pages render with Mirage removed entirely; no for Mirage on real routes.

sections.heading: I3 — Hot path is local
sections.text: No network call, disk wait or LLM call while handling a request. Decisions come from an in-memory snapshot, under a hard deadline. Loopback / unix socket calls to a local process with a hard deadline are allowed; remote calls are not. On timeout the adapter passes the request through. Test hooks: deadline-guard tests force a slow snapshot and assert the verdict degrades to observe + pass-through within the deadline budget.

sections.heading: I4 — Protected routes
sections.text: Login, checkout, API prefixes and anything the owner lists are never decoyed or throttled by decoy logic: the engine caps the verdict at tag on any protected route. The decoy catalog loader separately rejects duplicate entry paths and leads that would claim /.well-known/ or collide with an entry path. Test hooks: golden vectors v05/v09/v19 assert cap behavior; the pollution suite asserts no decoy appears on protected routes.

sections.heading: I5 — Bans are earned
sections.text: High-confidence signals only, short TTL, budget-capped, one-click reversible, always with reason codes. Structure signals alone can tag and throttle, never ban. Test hooks: vector set asserts no structure-only sequence reaches ban; enforce tests assert budget caps and reversibility.

sections.heading: I6 — Trusted client IP
sections.text: The real client IP is read only from proxies the owner explicitly trusts (uniformly, walking the chain right-to-left). Otherwise an attacker spoofs a header and gets innocent users banned. Test hooks: internal/model IP-extraction table tests cover chained spoofing; never-scored ranges (own IPs, CDN ranges) are listed in data.

sections.heading: I7 — Attacker data is hostile
sections.text: Every header, path and body that reaches logs, the dashboard or exports is untrusted input: escaped on output, length-capped, log-injection-safe. Test hooks: XSS/HTML-escaping tests on every render path; log-injection tests assert newlines and control characters cannot forge entries.

sections.heading: I8 — Decoys are inert
sections.text: Synthetic data only. Never real data, nothing executable, nothing that acts on the visitor's machine, no redirects to third parties. Test hooks: decoy validate suite rejects executable content, redirects and real-looking credentials.

sections.heading: I9 — Observe by default
sections.text: Enforcement is opt-in per site, and there is a global kill switch. Test hooks: config tests reject configs that enable enforcement without an explicit opt-in block; kill-switch tests assert DropToObserve within one interval.

sections.heading: I10 — Everything is explainable
sections.text: Each automated action stores its evidence: signals fired, weights, verdict, reason code, session key. Plain-English reason texts ship in data/reason-texts. Test hooks: every vector expectation carries a reason code; service tests assert stored events reference them.

sections.heading: I11 — Least privilege
sections.text: Connector tokens are scoped, never logged, never in the repo. Secrets come from the environment or a secret store. Test hooks: slop/secret grep gates the repo; connector tests assert tokens never appear in logs or errors.

sections.heading: I12 — No pollution of the public web
sections.text: Decoys are never indexable (X-Robots-Tag: noindex, nofollow, noarchive, robots.txt disallow, absent from sitemaps), never served to verified search engines, archivers or ordinary visitors, and served only to sessions already scored suspicious. Hidden-link injection never reaches verified crawlers. Test hooks: pollution suite crawls the test site as a verified bot and asserts zero decoy URLs; header assertions on every decoy response.

sections.heading: I13 — No misinformation, no junk content
sections.text: Decoys are inert technical artifacts — config files, fake admin shells, error pages — never articles, facts or claims about real people, brands or products. No plausible prose pages. Content scrapers are blocked or rate-limited; they are never fed garbage. Test hooks: catalog validation rejects prose-style decoys; brand/domain lint over the whole catalog.

sections.heading: I14 — No third-party harm
sections.text: Honeytokens never contain credentials that could work on a real service: formats that cannot validate, or registered canary tokens owned by the site owner. Decoy hostnames use reserved names only (example.com, .test, .invalid) and reserved ranges (192.0.2.0/24, 198.51.100.0/24, 203.0.113.0/24). No real brand names, no real personal data, no outbound links, no redirects. Test hooks: secret scanners and format validators run over the decoy catalog; reserved-host lint; vectors use reserved IPs only.

sections.heading: I15 — Blocklist hygiene
sections.text: Bans are local, short and expiring by default. Shared feeds, if ever offered, are opt-in, signed, corroborated, expiring, with appeals. Shared and carrier-grade NAT addresses, CDN ranges and addresses with recent legitimate sessions are never banned by default. Tor and VPN exits are tagged, not banned. A default ban covers a single address for minutes to hours, never a range. Test hooks: never-ban range table tests; ban record TTL tests; a feed-poisoning test asserts forged reports produce no ban.
